# Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning: The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory

Minghao Guo Qingyue Jiao Xiujin Liu Jianhong Pang Ruimeng Yang Naihao Xu

###### Abstract

Multimodal models and agents have emerged to enable AI systems to learn
from and interact with the real world more like humans by integrating
information across multiple modalities. However, enabling multimodal
agents to continually acquire useful information from complex,
heterogeneous multimodal data remains a significant challenge as they
move toward long-horizon tasks and lifelong settings. Addressing this
challenge requires effective memory mechanisms that can maintain
continuity across sessions, adapt to changing users and environments,
and refine memory-management policies through accumulated experience. We
introduce a two-axis analytical framework for multimodal agent memory
structured around two key questions: how multimodal information is
formed and represented (Axis I, _Formation and Representation_), and how
its management adapts with accumulated experience (Axis II, _Memory
Management_). Axis I, _Formation and Representation_, characterizes what
information is retained and how it is encoded (e.g., modality-specific
embeddings, textual and structured records, latent and parametric
representations) to support subsequent reasoning and action. Axis II,
_Memory Management_, distinguishes three tiers: T1 Static Memory reuses
fixed memory; T2 Dynamic Memory updates memory through a stable policy;
and T3 Self-Evolving Memory updates memory through an evolving policy.
Based on this framework, we synthesize recurring design patterns and
derive principles for balancing source fidelity with abstraction,
maintaining temporal validity and provenance, grounding memory use in
recoverable evidence, and evolving memory policies over time.
Furthermore, we discuss the challenges and potential future directions
for the memory mechanism of multimodal agents.

## 1 Introduction

Large foundation models ([OpenAI, 2026](#bib.bib163); [Anthropic,
2026](#bib.bib7); [DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026](#bib.bib35); [Google
DeepMind, 2026](#bib.bib52)), such as LLMs and MLLMs, have become the
reasoning and perception backbones of AI agents that interpret goals,
plan, use tools, and act through interaction with users and
environments. An agent places the model within a continuing loop of
observation, reasoning, and action ([Xi et al., 2025](#bib.bib245); [Wei
et al., 2026](#bib.bib231); [Plaat et al., 2025](#bib.bib167); [Chen,
Celia, 2026](#bib.bib28)), increasingly spanning multimodal digital and
physical environments. As this interaction unfolds over time, later
decisions often depend on information and experience accumulated beyond
the immediately available context. Memory provides the persistent state
that bridges these interactions, carrying relevant information from
prior observations and experience into subsequent reasoning and action
([Hu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib70); [Zhang et al., 2025e](#bib.bib289);
[Huang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib74)).

Memory is therefore a core component of AI agents ([Xu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib256); [Hu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib70)). At the most basic
level, it enables continuity by preserving task state and relevant
experience beyond the current interaction, allowing agents to operate
coherently over long horizons ([Packer et al., 2023](#bib.bib164)) and
across repeated interactions. Beyond continuity, persistent memory
allows agents to accumulate information over time, supporting
personalization through user-specific experience ([Hong et al.,
2026](#bib.bib67)) and maintaining consistent behavior as users, tasks,
and environments evolve ([Zhong et al., 2024](#bib.bib293)). By
retaining task outcomes, feedback ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib186)),
failure traces ([Tu et al., 2026](#bib.bib206)), and successful
strategies ([Fan et al., 2026b](#bib.bib43)), memory enables agents to
refine future decisions and accumulate reusable knowledge ([Li et al.,
2024](#bib.bib116)) and skills ([Wang et al., 2024a](#bib.bib210)).

The growing demand for agents that can interpret visual information
([Nguyen et al., 2026b](#bib.bib159); [Yu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib274)),
process temporally structured video and speech ([Lin et al.,
2026d](#bib.bib124); [Someki et al., 2026](#bib.bib189)), reason about
and navigate 3D spaces ([Gu et al., 2024](#bib.bib54)), and interact
with graphical and physical environments ([Agashe et al.,
2025](#bib.bib3); [Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib135)) has made multimodal
capabilities increasingly essential. To operate in these settings, an
agent must integrate heterogeneous, high-dimensional observations,
capture their temporal and spatial structure, and produce appropriate
actions or multimodal outputs ([Wang et al., 2024b](#bib.bib211)).
Unlike textual-only inputs, these multimodal observations cannot always
be compactly or losslessly reduced to a single representation for later
use. This shift does not merely increase the volume of experience an
agent may encounter; it changes the nature of what must be remembered
and organized. Consequently, multimodal memory must determine both what
aspects of experience should persist and how those retained memories
should remain useful as new observations accumulate and the underlying
world evolves.

To investigate these two requirements, we characterize multimodal agent
memory through a lifecycle with two coupled stages: formation determines
what experience is retained and in what representation, while management
governs how the resulting memory persists, changes, is accessed, and
guides later reasoning and action. These stages are tightly coupled:
decisions made during formation determine what evidence can later be
recovered, revised, or verified, while subsequent use and new
observations may require memories to be updated, reconciled,
consolidated, or forgotten. Multimodality makes both stages
substantially more challenging.

The first challenge arises during formation and representation: A
multimodal agent must decide what experience to retain, how to divide
continuous or heterogeneous observations into memory units, and in what
form those memories should persist. Unlike text-centered interactions,
which can be retained in a compact textual form that is directly
consumable and editable ([Packer et al., 2023](#bib.bib164); [Zhong et
al., 2024](#bib.bib293); [Chhikara et al., 2025](#bib.bib30)) by LLMs,
multimodal experience may contain perceptual, temporal, spatial, and
acoustic information that is expensive to preserve exhaustively and
difficult to compress without loss. A memory unit may correspond to an
image ([Nguyen et al., 2026b](#bib.bib159)), image region ([Wang et al.,
2026j](#bib.bib223)), video frame or clip ([Song et al.,
2024](#bib.bib190)), audiovisual event ([Lin et al.,
2026d](#bib.bib124)), object track ([Fan et al., 2024](#bib.bib44)),
interface state ([Wang and Chen, 2025](#bib.bib225)), action–observation
transition ([Zhang et al., 2026d](#bib.bib287)), trajectory ([Xu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib257)), or complete episode ([Zhang et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib283)). Each unit may be stored as source media ([Yu et
al., 2025c](#bib.bib274)), encoded as modality-specific features ([He et
al., 2024](#bib.bib61)) or geometric state ([Gu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib54)), abstracted into textual ([Feng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib46)) or structured records ([Long et al.,
2026](#bib.bib143)), compressed into a latent state ([Qian et al.,
2024](#bib.bib168)), or internalized in model parameters ([Suri et al.,
2026](#bib.bib200)). Each choice preserves some aspects of experience
while discarding or obscuring others, creating trade-offs among
fidelity, efficiency, editability, source recoverability, and
compatibility with downstream reasoning and action.

The second challenge arises during memory management: the memory state
formed from prior experience must remain valid as new observations
arrive, tasks progress, and environments change. The central question of
multimodal memory management is not only how the memory system responds
as its environment changes and experience accumulates, but also how to
reconcile heterogeneous and partial observations into a consistent,
evolving state. New evidence may extend an existing record ([Long et
al., 2026](#bib.bib143)), correct an earlier belief ([Ma et al.,
2026](#bib.bib148)), invalidate stale state ([Lei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib102)), connect previously separate events ([Yan et al.,
2026](#bib.bib261)), or provide feedback about the effectiveness of
prior memory decisions ([Bärmann et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)). Multimodal
memory management is particularly challenging because evidence is often
partial and viewpoint-dependent, while the same entity or event may be
represented across source media, modality-specific features, textual
summaries, and structured world states ([Fan et al., 2024](#bib.bib44)).
Effective management must reconcile new evidence across these linked
representations ([Feng et al., 2026](#bib.bib46)), preserve connections
to the supporting observations ([Lin et al., 2026d](#bib.bib124)), and
prevent stale or conflicting state from guiding later actions ([Yeo et
al., 2026b](#bib.bib269)). Memory systems differ in where persistent
adaptation occurs. Their responses may range from reusing formed memory
without persistent change ([Mu et al., 2026](#bib.bib156)), to updating
memory content or organization under a stable policy ([Mondal et al.,
2026](#bib.bib155)), to using feedback to improve and evolve the policy
governing future memory writing ([Zou et al., 2026a](#bib.bib297)),
maintenance ([Bärmann et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)), and retrieval ([Fan et
al., 2026b](#bib.bib43)).

Motivated by these lifecycle challenges, we present a unified analytical
framework for multimodal agent memory spanning images and documents,
video and audiovisual streams, audio and speech, GUI interaction, and
embodied or 3D environments. Our framework organizes the field along two
analytically distinct but operationally coupled axes, illustrated in
[Figure 1](#S1.F1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory").
Axis I, _Formation and Representation_, characterizes what experience is
retained, how it is organized into memory units, and the representation
ultimately supplied to downstream reasoning or action. We distinguish
source- and modality-specific representations, textual and structured
representations, and latent and parametric representations, while
separately examining hybrid architectures that combine multiple paths
and often link compact abstractions to recoverable source evidence. Axis
II, _Memory Management_, characterizes where persistent change occurs as
experience accumulates: T1 Static Memory systems reuse formed memory
without persistent modification; T2 Dynamic Memory systems update the
memory state through a stable management policy; and T3 Self-Evolving
Memory systems use feedback to update the policy governing future memory
writing, maintenance, or retrieval. Together, these axes capture both
what multimodal evidence survives into future computation and how the
memory system evolves through continued experience.

![Refer to
caption](2610.19366v1/multimodal-memory-lifecycle-illustrated.png)

Figure 1: Two complementary axes of multimodal agent memory. Axis I,
Formation and Representation, characterizes the memory representation
supplied to downstream computation. Axis II, Memory Management,
characterizes the scope of persistent change in memory state and

Beyond providing a unified taxonomy, this study offers three broader
contributions. First, we provide comprehensive coverage of multimodal
agent memory across modalities, tasks, architectures, and evaluation
settings, including a corpus of 297 memory architectures and 82
benchmark records in the current version of our taxonomy. Second, by
jointly analyzing memory representation and management, we identify
cross-cutting patterns that are difficult to observe from either
dimension alone, including the prevalence of dynamic memory updates, the
widespread use of hybrid representations, and the relative scarcity of
deployment-time memory-policy evolution. Third, we synthesize the
limitations of current systems and derive future directions around
recoverable and provenance-aware memory, temporal validity and
cross-representation consistency, self-improving memory management,
bounded lifelong memory, governed forgetting, and lifecycle-aware
evaluation.

This study focuses on memory mechanisms in multimodal agents. We define
memory as experience-derived state that persists beyond the step in
which it is formed and later affects reasoning, generation, planning, or
action. At least one non-text modality must contribute to its formation
or use; transient activations, one-pass reasoning traces, and incidental
prompt context are excluded unless explicitly persisted and reused.
Existing studies of agent memory classify memory by source ([Zhang et
al., 2025e](#bib.bib289)), representation ([Hu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib70); [Zhang et al., 2025e](#bib.bib289); [Du et al.,
2025](#bib.bib40)), function ([Hu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib70); [Wu et
al., 2025c](#bib.bib243); [Du et al., 2025](#bib.bib40)), temporal scope
([Wu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib243); [Du et al., 2025](#bib.bib40)), and
operation ([Zhang et al., 2025e](#bib.bib289); [Du et al.,
2025](#bib.bib40)), while others trace its evolution from storage to
reusable experience ([Hu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib70); [Huang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib74); [Luo et al., 2026a](#bib.bib145)). Multimodal
extensions cover LLM or MLLM memory types ([Jia et al.,
2025](#bib.bib82)), VLM taxonomies ([Xia et al., 2026a](#bib.bib247)),
and multimodal-agent architectures and storage ([Xie et al.,
2025](#bib.bib251); [Mokaria et al., 2026](#bib.bib154)), benchmarks
([Xie et al., 2025](#bib.bib251)), and applications ([Xie et al.,
2025](#bib.bib251); [Mokaria et al., 2026](#bib.bib154)). In contrast,
we shift the unit of analysis from memory components to the operational
lifecycle: how multimodal experience becomes persistent memory, how
representation constrains subsequent retrieval, revision, and
verification, and where adaptation occurs as experience accumulates.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
[Section 2](#S2 "2 Background ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
introduces the background, formal scope, and multimodal memory
lifecycle.
[Section 3](#S3 "3 Axis I: Formation and Representation ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
studies memory formation and representation, from source-preserving and
modality-native memory to explicit textual and structured
representations, latent and parametric memory, and hybrid source-linked
designs.
[Section 4](#S4 "4 Axis II: Memory Management ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
examines memory management across T1 Static Memory, T2 Dynamic Memory,
and T3 Self-Evolving Memory.
[Section 5](#S5 "5 Cross-Axis Analysis ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
analyzes how representation choices constrain memory management and
synthesizes corpus-level patterns across the two axes.
[Section 6](#S6 "6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
examines the systems mechanisms that realize these logical memory
designs under resource and coordination constraints.
[Section 7](#S7 "7 Evaluation and Applications ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
examines evaluation benchmarks and applications, while
[Section 8](#S8 "8 Challenges and Outlook ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
discusses open challenges and future directions.
[Section 9](#S9 "9 Conclusion ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
concludes the paper.

## 2 Background

![Refer to
caption](2610.19366v1/multimodal-agent-memory-publication-landscape.png)

Figure 2: Publication landscape of multimodal agent memory.
Representative methods across image, video, GUI, and embodied settings
from 2023 to 2026, organized by memory-management tier: T1 Static
Memory, T2 Dynamic Memory, and T3 Self-Evolving Memory.

Multimodal agents extend foundation vision-language models from one-shot
prediction to an interaction loop in which the system observes an
environment, reasons about a goal, selects an action, and interprets the
resulting state ([Xie et al., 2025](#bib.bib251); [Mokaria et al.,
2026](#bib.bib154)). Their observations may include text, images ([Deng
et al., 2026](#bib.bib36)), video ([Rege et al., 2026](#bib.bib175)),
audio ([Jiang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib86)), graphical interfaces ([Choi
et al., 2026](#bib.bib31)), robot poses ([Yan et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib262)), or other sensor streams ([Lin et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib123)). Because these inputs accumulate across steps and
often describe a changing world, the current context alone is rarely
sufficient for long-horizon reasoning. Memory provides continuity by
retaining selected information from earlier interaction and making it
available to later decisions.
[Figures 2](#S2.F2 "In 2 Background ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
and [3](#S2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 2 Background ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
summarize representative multimodal agent memory methods across
modalities, publication years, memory-management tiers, and their growth
over time.

Figure 3: Cumulative growth of multimodal-agent memory architectures
differs across modalities. Cumulative architecture counts in the
taxonomy-current corpus are plotted by publication year from 2023 to
2026 for embodied, video, image, GUI, and audio/speech modalities.
Embodied and video memory architectures show the steepest growth by
2026, followed by image and GUI systems, whereas audio/speech memory
remains comparatively sparse. The shaded interval highlights the recent
growth period after 2025.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

This definition includes external evidence stores ([Sun et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib197)), image and video banks ([Fan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib44)), maps ([Li et al., 2026i](#bib.bib113)), scene graphs
([Gu et al., 2024](#bib.bib54)), bounded visual buffers ([Wen et al.,
2026](#bib.bib236)), recurrent states explicitly designed as memory
([Wang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib227)), experience libraries ([Wang et al.,
2026g](#bib.bib220)), executable skills ([Wang et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib210)), and parameters generated or adapted for subsequent
reuse ([Suri et al., 2026](#bib.bib200)). It excludes ordinary
feed-forward activations, one-pass chains of thought, and incidental
prompt tokens when retained state and later reuse are not part of the
paper’s memory contribution.

This distinction separates memory from context. Context is the
information currently exposed to a model, whereas memory is the
mechanism that determines what information can survive, how it is
organized, and when it can re-enter the context or policy. A retrieved
image can therefore be both a stored memory item and part of the current
context, while an image seen once and immediately discarded is only an
observation. The distinction is especially important in multimodal
systems, where storing every perceptual input is computationally
impractical and often unnecessary.

In this study, we use source material to denote the external stream,
document, interaction, or environment from which an agent obtains
information. For each architecture, an observation is a bounded input
item made available to its memory-formation process at a particular
interaction step. We use evidence in a functional sense to describe an
observation or identifiable memory item that is used or made available
to support, ground, verify, or revise a claim, decision, action, or
memory state.

Text-based-agent research established many of the designs now reused by
multimodal systems: MemGPT ([Packer et al., 2023](#bib.bib164))
organizes working, recall, and archival memory; Generative Agents ([Park
et al., 2023](#bib.bib166)) transform observation streams into
higher-level reflections; MemoryBank ([Zhong et al., 2024](#bib.bib293))
combines dialogue history, user modeling, and forgetting; Reflexion
([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib186)) stores feedback as reusable
linguistic lessons; and Voyager ([Wang et al., 2024a](#bib.bib210))
preserves executable programs that can be retrieved and composed across
tasks. Together, these works show that memory may serve as a context
manager, a structured knowledge store, a reflective record, or a
procedural skill library.

Multimodal memory inherits these functions but introduces a more
difficult representation problem. Images contain spatial detail that may
not be captured by a caption ([Yu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib274)); video
and audio unfold continuously and must be segmented over time ([Zhang et
al., 2025d](#bib.bib285)); interface observations bind appearance to
actionable screen coordinates ([Choi et al., 2026](#bib.bib31)); and
embodied experience must be associated across viewpoints, object
identities, and changing locations ([Fan et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Wen
and Bekris, 2021](#bib.bib232); [Wen et al., 2023](#bib.bib234); [Xie et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib252)). As a result, the decision to retain a frame
([Yu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib271)), caption an event ([Wang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib226)), fuse a 3D map ([Zhu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib294)),
cache visual tokens ([Song et al., 2026](#bib.bib191)), or internalize
experience in parameters ([Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib133)) changes what
the agent can later recover.

Two broad strategies have emerged. Some systems preserve
modality-specific evidence or states so that later computation can
return to visual ([Shlapentokh-Rothman et al., 2026](#bib.bib187)),
auditory ([Someki et al., 2026](#bib.bib189)), or geometric information
([Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib135)). Others translate experience into
language ([Feng et al., 2026](#bib.bib46)), structured symbols ([Long et
al., 2026](#bib.bib143)), shared latent spaces ([Yu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib275)), or parameters ([Suri et al., 2026](#bib.bib200))
that are easier to search and reuse. Native preservation keeps a wider
range of perceptual detail but increases storage and retrieval cost.
Translation produces compact and editable memory units but can remove
information that was not anticipated when the memory was constructed.
This trade-off motivates our memory formation and representation axis.

### 2.1 Classical Memory in AI & Cognitive Science

Memory has long been viewed as a requirement for intelligent behavior.
In cognitive science, models often distinguish between short-lived
perceptual storage, limited-capacity working memory ([Baddeley and
Hitch, 1974](#bib.bib10)), and more durable long-term memory ([Atkinson
and Shiffrin, 1968](#bib.bib9)). This view suggests that memory is not
only a place to keep information, but also a mechanism for selecting,
organizing, and using information during reasoning and action.

Cognitive theories also distinguish memory by function. Episodic memory
stores experiences tied to particular events, while semantic memory
stores general knowledge that can be reused across contexts ([Tulving,
1972](#bib.bib207)). Procedural memory supports skills and action
routines ([Squire, 1992](#bib.bib192)). These distinctions are useful
for agent systems because memory may preserve specific past experience
([Li et al., 2026g](#bib.bib111)), provide reusable abstractions ([Li et
al., 2026c](#bib.bib106)), or support future behavior ([Qin et al.,
2026](#bib.bib170)).

Classical AI studied memory from a computational perspective. Symbolic
systems represented knowledge as facts, rules, frames, scripts, or
production rules, while cognitive architectures such as SOAR ([Newell,
1990](#bib.bib157)) and ACT-R ([Anderson et al., 2004](#bib.bib6))
placed memory inside a control loop for problem solving and decision
making. Case-based reasoning made experience reuse explicit by solving
new problems through the retrieval and adaptation of past cases ([Aamodt
and Plaza, 1994](#bib.bib1)). These ideas anticipate many concerns in
modern agent memory, including indexing ([Zhu et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib296)), retrieval ([Qiu et al., 2026](#bib.bib171)),
consolidation ([Chen et al., 2026c](#bib.bib22)), forgetting ([Mi et
al., 2026](#bib.bib152)), and reuse ([He et al., 2026](#bib.bib63)).

Neural models changed the implementation of memory. Recurrent networks
store information in hidden states ([Hochreiter and Schmidhuber,
1997](#bib.bib65)), while attention-based models can use the context as
temporary memory ([Vaswani et al., 2017](#bib.bib208)). Memory-augmented
neural networks further introduce external modules that can be read and
written during computation ([Graves et al., 2014](#bib.bib53); [Weston
et al., 2015](#bib.bib238)). For modern agents, the central issue is
therefore not only how information is represented internally, but also
what experience persists beyond the current computation and how that
retained information is later accessed or changed. This perspective
connects classical memory research to the two functional stages
considered in this study: formation and representation, which determine
what experience is retained and in what form it reaches downstream
computation, and memory management, which determines how retained memory
is accessed, maintained, and adapted over time.

### 2.2 Foundations of Modern Agentic Memory

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) provides an important conceptual
foundation for modern agentic memory by separating model parameters from
an external, queryable information source ([Lewis et al.,
2020](#bib.bib103)). At inference time, retrieved evidence is introduced
into the model context, enabling access to information beyond parametric
knowledge and the current input. In its standard form, however, RAG
primarily addresses how stored information is accessed. It does not by
itself specify how an agent should form memory from its own experience,
maintain that memory over time, or revise it through later interactions.

Modern agent memory broadens this retrieval-centered view by treating
prior interaction and experience as persistent state that can be
retained, transformed, and reused across tasks or sessions. Systems such
as MemGPT ([Packer et al., 2023](#bib.bib164)), Generative Agents ([Park
et al., 2023](#bib.bib166)), and MemoryBank ([Zhong et al.,
2024](#bib.bib293)) helped establish this shift from external knowledge
retrieval toward persistent experience management. Taken together, these
systems move memory beyond factual retrieval toward persistence,
transformation, and experience reuse across interactions. They provide
conceptual foundations for multimodal agent memory, where the same
problems arise over richer forms of experience and a broader range of
representations.

When considering how long-horizon agents retain and use information
accumulated over extended interactions, it is important to distinguish
three closely related concepts: _long-context processing_, _context
management_, and _memory_. Long-context processing refers to a model’s
capacity to capture and use information distributed across extended
input sequences at manageable computational cost. Context management
determines which information is included in the active context at each
inference step and how it is presented to the model. Memory, as defined
in this study, denotes experience-derived state that persists beyond the
current inference step and subsequently influences reasoning,
generation, planning, or action. Depending on its representation and
integration, memory can support long-context processing by carrying
historical information across input segments and support context
management by selecting relevant memory content as context for the
model. Long-context processing and memory augmentation serve
complementary aspects for building long-horizon and lifelong agents:
memory extends access to information beyond the active context, while
long-context models integrate retained information from memory into
current computation ([Wu et al., 2022](#bib.bib244); [He et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib64)). Beyond these functions, persistent memory enables
agents to accumulate experience across interactions, tasks, and
sessions, providing a substrate for inference-time adaptation and
longer-term agent evolution.

### 2.3 The Multimodal Memory Lifecycle

![Refer to caption](2610.19366v1/embodied-memory-lifecycle-taxonomy.png)

Figure 4: The multimodal memory lifecycle illustrated through a
household-robot example. The same experience forms alternative memory
representations, managed as Static, Dynamic, or Self-Evolving Memory,
and later accessed and used for action.

{forest}

Figure 5: Taxonomy of multimodal agent memory along two complementary
axes: Formation and Representation, and Memory Management. T1 Static
Memory stores and reuses fixed memory; T2 Dynamic Memory updates memory
through a stable policy; T3 Self-Evolving Memory updates memory through
an evolving policy. Representative systems may incorporate multiple
mechanisms across memory lifecycle stages and therefore appear in
multiple categories.

Multimodal agent memory can be understood through two coupled functional
stages: (1) formation and representation and (2) memory management.
Formation determines what experience is retained, how it is organized,
and the representation through which it becomes available to downstream
computation. Memory management determines how the resulting state
persists, changes, is accessed, and is used during deployment. These
stages form a lifecycle rather than independent modules: management is
constrained by what formation preserves, while the outcomes of memory
use may trigger further formation, revision, consolidation, or
forgetting.
[Figure 4](#S2.F4 "In 2.3 The Multimodal Memory Lifecycle ‣ 2 Background ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
illustrates the two coupled stages of multimodal agent memory and the
three memory-management tiers through a household-robot example.

##### Formation and Representation.

The first stage, formation and representation, determines what
experience is saved as memory, how it is organized into memory units,
and how those units are represented. The definition of a memory unit
varies across modalities and levels of granularity. For static images, a
unit can be an entire image, region, object, or scene ([Nguyen et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib159); [Wang et al., 2026j](#bib.bib223)). For video and
audio, it may correspond to a keyframe, clip, event, object track, or
temporally aligned audiovisual segment ([Song et al.,
2024](#bib.bib190); [Lin et al., 2026d](#bib.bib124)). In embodied
settings, memory units may further capture multimodal observations,
estimated world and object states, action-observation transitions,
trajectories, or complete interaction ([Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib135);
[Zhang et al., 2026d](#bib.bib287); [Weng et al., 2024](#bib.bib237)).
Once these units are formed, the agent may preserve raw or compressed
sensory evidence ([Fan et al., 2024](#bib.bib44)), encode
modality-native features or tokens ([He et al., 2024](#bib.bib61)),
translate perceptual observations into textual or structured symbolic
records ([Feng et al., 2026](#bib.bib46)), organize spatial and temporal
relations as event graphs, scene graphs, or spatial maps ([Gu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib54)), encode accumulated experience in recurrent latent
states ([Qian et al., 2024](#bib.bib168)), or internalize it through
updates to model parameters ([Suri et al., 2026](#bib.bib200)).

##### Memory Management.

The second stage governs how formed memories are retained, updated,
accessed, and used during deployment. Axis II distinguishes three tiers
according to whether the memory state and the policy that manages it
change during use. _T1: Static Memory_ stores and reuses fixed memory
without modifying its content, organization, access indices, or
metadata. _T2: Dynamic Memory_ updates the memory state through a stable
management policy, including appending new observations ([Liu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib135)), revising existing state ([Feng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib46)), merging redundant entries ([Song et al.,
2024](#bib.bib190)), consolidating repeated evidence ([Li et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib105)), invalidating outdated information ([Liu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib127)), and forgetting under capacity constraints ([Xiao
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib250)). _T3: Self-Evolving Memory_ updates the
memory state while also revising the policy that governs memory writing,
maintenance, or access in response to feedback. Access includes the
retrieval ([Zhang et al., 2026e](#bib.bib288)), routing ([Sun et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib196)), or activation ([Wang et al., 2026h](#bib.bib221))
mechanisms that make relevant memory available to current computation.
Utilization determines how the accessed information is incorporated into
reasoning, generation, planning, action, or learning. These processes
form a coupled management loop but remain distinct failure points: an
agent may fail to retrieve relevant evidence, retrieve it but apply it
incorrectly, or produce a correct output from model priors without using
memory ([Tang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib203); [Rathi, 2026](#bib.bib174)).
Management is also constrained by formation and representation: no
access mechanism can recover information that was discarded during
formation or subsequently corrupted, invalidated, or forgotten.

Axis I, _Formation and Representation_, classifies the memory
representation through which retained experience becomes available to
downstream computation. Axis II, _Memory Management_, classifies systems
by the scope of persistent deployment-time change they support in memory
state and management policy. The resulting taxonomy is summarized in
[Figure 5](#S2.F5 "In 2.3 The Multimodal Memory Lifecycle ‣ 2 Background ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory").

## 3 Axis I: Formation and Representation

![Refer to
caption](2610.19366v1/multimodal-memory-representation-taxonomy.png)

Figure 6: Representations in multimodal agent memory. Multimodal
experience may be retained close to the source modality, transformed
into explicit textual or structured records, or internalized as latent
states or parametric memory. We classify each memory path by the
representation ultimately supplied to downstream computation, rather
than by formats used only for storage or indexing. These families expose
recurring trade-offs among recoverability, interpretability,
compactness, and tight integration with the agent policy. Hybrid
architectures combine multiple representations, often linking compact
abstractions to recoverable source evidence.

In Axis I, we examine how multimodal experience forms persistent memory
and the representations that will be retrieved and used in future
reasoning or action. As summarized in
[Figure 6](#S3.F6 "In 3 Axis I: Formation and Representation ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory"),
we classify by the representation ultimately supplied to the reasoner or
action policy, rather than merely by the format used as retrieval index.
Formation mechanisms determine the representational form in which raw
experiences are encoded and retained as memory. This process creates
distinct memory units and determines what information remains available
for subsequent use. The same image, video, audio stream, or embodied
episode may be retained as source evidence ([Fan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib44)), transformed into modality-specific visual tokens
([Song et al., 2024](#bib.bib190)), acoustic features ([Wu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib240)), temporally organized video features ([He et al.,
2024](#bib.bib61)), or geometric state ([Gu et al., 2024](#bib.bib54)),
abstracted into linguistic ([Yin et al., 2026](#bib.bib270)), symbolic
([Jiang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib85)), relational ([Long et al.,
2026](#bib.bib143)), or executable records ([Wang et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib210)), or maintained as persistent latent state ([Qian et
al., 2024](#bib.bib168)) or knowledge encoded in model parameters ([Suri
et al., 2026](#bib.bib200)). Accordingly, we organize this axis into
three families.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Many systems combine multiple representations ([Yan et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib262); [Li et al., 2026g](#bib.bib111); [Huang et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib75)). For example, a system might use a semantic graph to
locate compressed visual features and then reopen the source image for
verification ([Fan et al., 2024](#bib.bib44); [Long et al.,
2026](#bib.bib143)). We therefore discuss _hybrid and evidence-linked
architectures_ separately as system-level compositions rather than as a
fourth representation type.

### 3.1 Source- and Modality-Specific Representations

At the least abstract end of the representation axis, multimodal
experiences are saved in their originating modality. We distinguish two
forms. _Retained source evidence_ preserves images ([Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib279)), video or audio segments ([Liu et al.,
2026j](#bib.bib137)), and sensor observations ([Dorbala and Manocha,
2026](#bib.bib39)) as media that the agent can reopen during inference.
_Modality-native encodings_ instead retain learned features ([Diko et
al., 2025](#bib.bib38)), tokens ([Zhao et al., 2025a](#bib.bib290)), or
geometric state ([Honerkamp et al., 2024](#bib.bib66)) that preserve
modality-specific structure without requiring the original media to be
processed again. Both avoid reducing experience to language or symbolic
records, but they serve different priorities: source evidence remains
directly verifiable and interpretable, whereas encoded state is more
compact and computationally efficient but is often lossy and difficult
to interpret.

#### 3.1.1 Retained Perceptual Source Evidence

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Depending on the input, these items may be complete images ([Nguyen et
al., 2026b](#bib.bib159)), regions or crops ([Choi et al.,
2026](#bib.bib31)), document screenshots ([Yu et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib274)), sampled video frames ([Zhang et al.,
2025d](#bib.bib285)), audiovisual segments ([Lin et al.,
2026d](#bib.bib124)), RGB-D observations ([Yang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib265)), or observations paired with timestamps and agent
poses ([Yan et al., 2025b](#bib.bib262)).

For static images and graphical user interfaces (GUIs), retaining visual
evidence preserves layout, typography, color, fine-grained appearance,
and spatial organization that textualization may discard ([Yu et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib274); [Wang et al., 2026j](#bib.bib223)). PixelRAG ([Wang
et al., 2026j](#bib.bib223)), for example, renders webpages as
screenshot tiles, indexes them using visual embeddings, and supplies the
highest-ranked tiles directly to a VLM as pixel inputs. In this case,
the embeddings serve only as a retrieval index, whereas the retrieved
screenshots constitute the source-level visual evidence made available
during inference. Source-evidence memory can also operate at different
granularities: related systems retain complete screenshots ([Liu et al.,
2025d](#bib.bib141)), action-relevant GUI regions ([Choi et al.,
2026](#bib.bib31)), cropped interface elements ([Zeng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib278)) , or complete visual interaction histories with
frame- and region-level access ([Han et al., 2026](#bib.bib60)), and
selectively retrieve the visual observations most relevant to the
current decision.

Video and audio pose an additional access challenge because relevant
evidence must first be localized within a continuous temporal stream.
Existing systems address this challenge through different organizational
structures ([Lian et al., 2026](#bib.bib118)). ToolMerge
([Shlapentokh-Rothman et al., 2026](#bib.bib187)) retains sampled video
frames and uses an LLM planner to compose complementary visual retrieval
tools, including global image-text matching, region-level entity
matching, and OCR. HippoMM ([Lin et al., 2026d](#bib.bib124)) adopts an
event-centered organization, where audiovisual experience is segmented
into event records with semantic summaries, temporal boundaries, and
pointers to source spans. M3-Agent ([Long et al., 2026](#bib.bib143))
instead organizes memory around persistent entities, linking text,
image, and audio evidence to people, objects, and events over time.
These designs correspond to frame-, event-, and entity-level
organization, respectively, showing that retaining source media is only
one part of the problem; the evidence must also be indexed at a
granularity suited to later retrieval.

Spatial indexing plays a similar role in embodied agents ([Li et al.,
2026e](#bib.bib109)). GraphEQA ([Saxena et al., 2025](#bib.bib179))
combines a hierarchical 3D scene graph with a task-relevant memory of
images captured during exploration, allowing retrieved images to restore
local visual details that may be abstracted away in the global graph.
DovSG ([Yan et al., 2025b](#bib.bib262)) associates RGB-D observations
and camera poses with a dynamic object-level map so that historical
observations can support relocalization and local map refinement when
the environment changes. These systems show that source evidence and
structured spatial memory serve complementary roles: the structured
representation supports compact, global reasoning, while linked
observations preserve detailed perceptual evidence for inspection,
grounding, and update.

The primary advantage of preserving source-modality evidence is
recoverability: information retained in the original observation can be
retrieved at different levels of granularity for later uses that may not
have been anticipated during memory formation. This preserves
fine-grained visual details, temporal structure ([Zuo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib299)), acoustic cues ([Someki et al., 2026](#bib.bib189)),
and observational context ([Anwar et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)), while also
allowing later reasoning and actions to be grounded in and checked
against specific observations.

#### 3.1.2 Modality-Specific Encodings and Geometric State

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Retaining source observations maximizes recoverability, but storing,
retrieving, and repeatedly encoding every image, video frame, audio
segment, or sensor observation can be prohibitively expensive for
long-running agents. A more compact strategy is to persist encoded
features or geometric state. We assign a memory architecture to this
category when the stored value is itself consumed by the reasoner or
action policy and preserves task-relevant structure inherited from the
originating modality, such as spatial organization, temporal order,
acoustic dynamics, or metric geometry.

Video provides the clearest setting for modality-specific encoded memory
because long streams require compact representations that preserve both
spatial and temporal information. Representative systems differ mainly
in the granularity and consolidation strategy of the retained features.
MovieChat ([Song et al., 2024](#bib.bib190)) accumulates frame-level
visual tokens in a fixed-capacity short-term memory and repeatedly
merges similar representations from temporally adjacent frames before
transferring the consolidated features to long-term memory. MA-LMM ([He
et al., 2024](#bib.bib61)) instead stores patch-level features in a
visual memory bank, where they directly serve as keys and values for
cross-attention; when capacity is exceeded, temporally adjacent features
are merged at corresponding spatial locations. Flash-VStream ([Zhang et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib282)) uses a coarse-to-fine design in which
low-resolution feature centroids provide broad temporal coverage and
high-resolution feature maps preserve detail for representative key
frames. At query time, these features are combined according to their
temporal positions and supplied to the language model through the visual
projector. These systems illustrate three forms of encoded video memory:
temporally consolidated frame tokens, spatially aligned patch features,
and coarse-to-fine representations of a continuing stream. Despite their
different structures, all persist visual features as the memory records
itself rather than merely as retrieval indices for source frames.
Modality-specific encoding can therefore limit memory growth while
retaining spatial and temporal structure needed for later inference,
although the resulting memory remains tied to a compatible model
interface.

Image memory follows a different pattern. Representative agent systems
more commonly retain decodable source images or pointers to them and use
visual embeddings only for indexing and retrieval ([Nguyen et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib158); [Deng et al., 2026](#bib.bib36)). M3-Agent ([Long
et al., 2026](#bib.bib143)), for example, stores image content alongside
embeddings used for similarity-based retrieval, while M²A ([Feng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib46)) associates stored images with textual captions and
cross-modal embeddings that support both text- and image-based search.
Other systems transform visual observations into textual ([Gao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib48)) or structured records ([Wen et al.,
2024](#bib.bib235)) and discard the source images. UniversalRAG ([Yeo et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib268)) extends this indexing pattern across
heterogeneous corpora by routing queries to modality- and
granularity-specific retrievers. MIRIX ([Wang and Chen,
2025](#bib.bib225)) follows this approach for screenshot-based memory.
These designs show that image encoders frequently support memory
formation and retrieval, but their feature vectors less commonly serve
as persistent memory values consumed directly by the downstream model.

Persistent encoded audio memory remains underexplored among the analyzed
systems. Unlike speaker embeddings used only as retrieval keys ([Yao et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib267)), such memory would preserve acoustic
information as the stored value and expose it directly to the downstream
model. OMAC ([Wu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib240)), introduced in O-MARC,
provides a relevant encoding mechanism. It retains high-importance audio
tokens as anchors and merges nearby discarded tokens into them through
weighted aggregation. The resulting tokens remain temporally ordered and
are consumed directly by a compatible omnimodal backbone without
reconstructing the original waveform. OMAC therefore illustrates how
acoustic features could serve as memory unit values rather than
retrieval indices. However, it compresses the current audiovisual
context rather than preserving information across interactions, so it is
better viewed as a transferable representation mechanism than as an
established example of persistent agent memory. This distinction also
highlights how little persistent audio-feature memory has been explored
relative to its visual counterpart.

Embodied agents extend modality-specific memory from neural feature
sequences to world-centered geometric state ([Huang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib72); [Zhu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib294)). DynaMem ([Liu et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib135)) converts posed RGB-D observations into an
evolving sparse voxel map in a global coordinate frame. Its voxels
combine metric location, observation history, timestamps, and
vision-language features, while new depth observations update or remove
inconsistent state. This structure preserves metric relations and
occupancy changes that would be difficult to recover from an unordered
feature collection. A different design is to retain perceptual history
for action generation rather than to construct an explicit world model.
MemoryVLA ([Shi et al., 2026a](#bib.bib184)) compresses visual-encoder
outputs into perceptual tokens that query a temporally indexed long-term
bank. Retrieved history is fused with the current perceptual state and
used to condition the action policy, while capacity is controlled by
merging similar temporally adjacent entries. The resulting bank
therefore stores a bounded history of policy-relevant visual features
without reconstructing source observations. The key distinction lies in
the role of memory: DynaMem organizes memory around persistent world
geometry, whereas MemoryVLA organizes it around perceptual history
required by the control policy.

Across these systems, the representation is decided by the structure
required by the downstream interface. Video memories preserve spatial
and temporal organization ([He et al., 2024](#bib.bib61)), emerging
acoustic encodings retain temporally localized sound information ([Wu et
al., 2026b](#bib.bib240)), geometric maps expose metric layout and
occupancy ([Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib135)), and policy-facing memories
retain action-relevant perceptual history ([Shi et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib184)). Persisting these representations reduces storage,
context, and repeated encoding costs while preserving information that
may be difficult to express through language or symbolic records. The
resulting compression is generally non-invertible: information removed
through sampling ([Yu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib272)), merging ([Song et
al., 2026](#bib.bib191)), clustering ([Zhang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib282)), spatial reduction ([Guo et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib55)), or voxelization ([Lin et al., 2026c](#bib.bib123))
cannot be recovered from the encoded state alone. Learned feature
memories are also model-specific and normally require a compatible
projector, Q-Former, attention module, or policy interface. Geometric
state is more explicitly structured, but discretization and feature
aggregation can still remove perceptual detail. Modality-specific
encodings and geometric state therefore trade recoverability and
portability for compact, task-aligned access to perceptual and spatial
structure.

### 3.2 Cross-Represented Explicit Memory

Multimodal experience can also be transformed into natural language or
structured representations such as knowledge graphs. For example, an
image may be stored as a caption ([Feng et al., 2026](#bib.bib46)),
while an embodied observation may be represented as a scene graph
containing nodes and relations between them ([Gu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib54)). Because the relevant content is expressed through
readable text or named graph components, it can be directly retrieved
and used for reasoning or action. Compared with modality-specific
encodings and latent or parametric memory, these representations can
usually be inspected, searched, edited, or invalidated at the level of
individual entries. However, their construction is also lossy: detailed
visual information omitted during captioning, entity extraction, or
relation construction usually cannot be recovered from the resulting
representation alone.

Within _Cross-Represented Explicit Memory_, _Perception-to-Text Records
and Summaries_ translate multimodal experience into natural-language
entries that are retrieved and supplied to the agent as text. Although
these entries may be indexed by timestamps, identifiers, or embedding
similarity, the content placed in the backbone LLM’s context remains
textual. _Spatial, Temporal, and Cross-Modal Structured Memory_
organizes information as graph-linked entities and relations or
schema-defined fields that can be queried and updated individually. For
example, a vector database of captions is textual memory, whereas a
scene graph is structured memory when its nodes, relations, or topology
support retrieval, reasoning, or action. Because a single architecture
may combine multiple representation forms, we discuss each form in its
respective section rather than assigning the architecture as a whole to
a single category.

#### 3.2.1 Perception-to-Text Records and Summaries

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Textual memory expresses past experience as descriptions ([Jain et al.,
2025](#bib.bib78)), event records ([Zhang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib286)),
summaries ([Rasheed and Kabtoul, 2026](#bib.bib173)), facts ([Liu et
al., 2026g](#bib.bib132)), profiles ([Wang and Chen,
2025](#bib.bib225)), or natural-language procedures ([Fan et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib43)). Its memory unit is a linguistic entry that can be
retrieved through semantic similarity, lexical matching, temporal
filtering, or structured querying and then inserted directly into an LLM
context. This representation aligns naturally with language-model
reasoning and permits human inspection and correction without requiring
a decoder. Textual memory is also well suited to evolving state because
updates, corrections, and overrides can be directly incorporated into
compact, ordered records, whereas modifying or reconciling multimodal
evidence and its embeddings is less straightforward . It also separates
storage from the original perception model: a textual memory produced by
one visual or audio encoder can generally be read by another language
model.

Long video provides a clear setting for this strategy because retaining
every frame is expensive, while many downstream questions concern
events, actions, and state changes that can be summarized
linguistically. VideoAgent ([Fan et al., 2024](#bib.bib44)) constructs a
compact semantic memory of temporal event descriptions and allows an LLM
agent to query these records while deciding when additional visual
evidence is needed. Video-EM ([Wang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib226)) makes
the event abstraction more explicit. It localizes potentially relevant
moments, groups them into temporally coherent events, and writes
grounded episodic records containing temporal indices and when, where,
what, and who cues. A chain-of-thought retrieval process then selects a
minimal set of event memories for answering the current question. ReMA
([Chen et al., 2026a](#bib.bib20)) processes a lifelong video stream as
fixed-duration clips, writes timestamp-aligned descriptions into a
vector-indexed memory bank, and merges temporally overlapping
observations into updated summaries. Its controller later searches these
textual records and adds the results of query-directed inspections back
into the same belief state. Across these systems, linguistic abstraction
changes the basic memory unit from a frame to a semantically delimited
event or observation, allowing temporally distant evidence to be
addressed without repeatedly processing the complete video.

Textual memory is also prominent in GUI agents, where screenshots and
interactions can be converted into persistent facts ([Gao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib48)), events ([Liu et al., 2025d](#bib.bib141)), and
workflows ([Mi et al., 2026](#bib.bib152)). MIRIX ([Wang and Chen,
2025](#bib.bib225)) filters visually redundant screenshots and routes
new screen and conversational evidence to specialized memory managers.
These managers construct natural-language summaries, event details,
semantic records, workflow steps, document excerpts, and user-profile
facts across six memory components. During retrieval, the system
searches these components using embedding-, BM25-, or string-based
methods, and the selected entries are ultimately supplied to the chat
agent as labeled text. The resulting representation abstracts transient
interface appearance into concepts that remain useful across later
interactions, such as user activities, previously accessed resources, or
recurring workflows.

Persistent image memory is less commonly represented solely in text. A
single image is comparatively inexpensive to retain, while future
queries may depend on typography, color, layout, object appearance, or
fine spatial relations that cannot always be anticipated when a caption
is written. Purely textual image memory is therefore most useful when
images occur as part of a longer personal or interaction history, such
as a screenshot stream or camera roll ([Wang and Chen,
2025](#bib.bib225); [Nguyen et al., 2026a](#bib.bib158)), and the
relevant memory objects are people, activities, events, or preferences
rather than arbitrary visual details. In such settings, captions and
event summaries provide efficient semantic access, while source images
can be retained separately when later visual verification is required
([Jiang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib84)). This pattern explains why text-only
image memory is less dominant than textual event memory for long video
and interaction histories.

Pure textual memory is less common for embodied experience as well. Text
can summarize observed events and completed tasks, but embodied action
often depends on precise and current information about object locations,
metric distances, containment, connectivity, and other spatial relations
that cannot be reliably reconstructed from isolated free-form text
records. Embodied systems therefore typically associate linguistic
descriptions with spatial maps or entity-centered state rather than
relying on unstructured text alone ([Riva et al., 2026](#bib.bib178);
[Lei et al., 2025](#bib.bib102)). Textual records remain valuable for
episodic histories, task outcomes, and high-level instructions, while
localization and planning generally rely on the structured
representations discussed in the next section.

Across modalities, textualization provides a compact and interpretable
interface between perception and reasoning. It supports semantic
retrieval, direct insertion into model context, human editing, and
consolidation of observations across modalities. Its primary limitation
is the semantic bottleneck introduced when memories are written.
Captions and summaries retain information judged salient by the
formation model, but may omit visual details, flatten temporal or
spatial relationships, discard acoustic cues, or introduce unsupported
interpretations. Because retrieval cannot recover information that was
never encoded in the textual record, the quality of textual memory
depends not only on retrieval accuracy but also on the coverage,
grounding, and factual reliability of the textualization process.

#### 3.2.2 Spatial, Temporal, and Cross-Modal Structured Memory

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Graphs and structured records represent experience through explicitly
organized and addressable entities ([Zhang et al., 2025c](#bib.bib283)),
attributes ([Sun et al., 2026e](#bib.bib199)), relations ([Jiang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib83)), state variables ([Wang et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib228)), temporal links ([Chang and Ren,
2026](#bib.bib18)), or spatial structures ([Honerkamp et al.,
2024](#bib.bib66)). Their meaning derives not only from the content of
individual nodes or records but also from the relationships and
organization among them. Accordingly, access may involve field-level
lookup, graph traversal, temporal filtering, relational propagation, or
spatial queries, rather than treating each entry as an independent text
passage. Such representations are particularly valuable when an agent
must determine not only what occurred, but also how entities are
related, which state is currently valid, or where an action should be
executed.

Embodied agents provide particularly clear examples of structured
memory, as navigation and manipulation often require persistent
representations of objects, their spatial and functional relationships,
and, in dynamic environments, changes in scene state over time.
ConceptGraphs ([Gu et al., 2024](#bib.bib54)) lifts open-vocabulary
detections from successive RGB-D observations into a 3D coordinate frame
and incrementally fuses them into object nodes and relational edges. The
resulting scene graph supports language-grounded, object-centric, and
spatial access, allowing an agent to retrieve entities and their
locations for downstream perception and planning. DovSG ([Yan et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib262)) extends this design to changing environments. It
maintains persistent 3D object nodes with geometric and semantic
features, connects them through spatial relations, and locally refines
regions affected by robot interactions or environmental changes. The
task planner reads target coordinates, object features, and graph
relations to decompose instructions and support navigation, grasping,
and placement. In this case, the graph is not merely an index over
observations; it is the current world state on which planning operates.
GraphEQA ([Saxena et al., 2025](#bib.bib179)) demonstrates how
structured spatial memory can guide active information acquisition.
During exploration, it incrementally constructs a hierarchical 3D
metric-semantic scene graph containing object, room, and frontier
information. The graph exposes what has already been observed, how the
explored space is organized, and where additional evidence may be
obtained. This state is supplied to a VLM planner that decides whether
the available memory is sufficient to answer the question or whether the
agent should continue exploring. Structured spatial memory therefore
supports both retrospective access and prospective action: it preserves
previously acquired observations while guiding the agent toward
locations where additional evidence can be gathered.

Video agents impose similar structure on temporal experience. PyraVid
([Yan et al., 2026](#bib.bib261)) organizes streaming video into a
three-level graph comprising fine-grained fact nodes, clip-level
summaries, and a global narrative. Hierarchical aggregation edges
connect facts to clips and clips to the global memory, while additional
logical links connect related evidence across time. Retrieval begins
from query-relevant seed nodes, checks whether the evidence is
sufficient, and traverses the graph to expand or prune the active
evidence set. WorldMM ([Yeo et al., 2026b](#bib.bib269)) constructs
multiple temporal knowledge graphs from video segments at different
resolutions and an evolving semantic graph from consolidated
entity-action-entity triplets. Episodic access uses graph-based
Personalized PageRank followed by cross-scale reranking, while semantic
access performs edge-focused traversal over the consolidated graph. New
triplets can update or remove outdated and conflicting relations. These
systems show how explicit temporal and relational structure can preserve
event dependencies that would be difficult to recover from an unordered
collection of captions.

For persistent image memory, structured representations are particularly
useful when an agent must track entities and their attributes across
multiple observations. TAME ([Hong et al., 2026](#bib.bib67)), for
example, maintains a Dynamic State Memory for transient or changing
attributes and a Static Personalized Memory for stable attributes, both
indexed by personalized concept identifiers. Attributes that remain
stable can migrate from dynamic to static memory, while outdated
attributes are removed from the bounded dynamic store. During retrieval,
the system identifies the personalized concept in the current image and
retrieves its associated attributes from both memories. Separating
dynamic from stable attributes helps the agent distinguish transient
observations, such as a recent appearance or condition, from persistent
user-specific properties.

Structured visual memory can also encode the presence status of
remembered concepts. PolarMem ([Chen et al., 2026h](#bib.bib27))
constructs a polarized graph that links visual memories to concept nodes
through HAS and NOT_HAS edges, thereby distinguishing verified presence
from verified absence. At query time, its logic-aware retrieval
procedure enforces logical consistency before ranking candidates by
semantic similarity. Memories that conflict with the query constraints
are therefore suppressed even when they are semantically similar.
PolarMem thus demonstrates that graph structure can represent not only
associations among memory items but also positive and negative evidence.
This capability is particularly valuable when an agent must explicitly
rule out concepts that are visually plausible but absent from the
observed evidence.

Persistent structured memory is also relatively uncommon in GUI agents.
Although a GUI presents structured elements at any given moment, its
layout and element hierarchy may change across application versions,
window sizes, navigation states, and dynamically generated content.
Memories tied to absolute screen coordinates or specific interface
graphs may therefore generalize poorly across tasks and sessions. Most
GUI agents more commonly retain textual interaction histories ([Agashe
et al., 2025](#bib.bib3)) or parameterized workflow templates ([Xiao et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib249)) that abstract away from a particular interface
configuration. When structured GUI memory is used, it therefore tends to
represent task state ([Wang et al., 2024c](#bib.bib212)), interface
entities ([Yu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib273)), or reusable procedures ([Lee
et al., 2024](#bib.bib98)) rather than a persistent geometric map of the
interface.

Graphs and structured records support compositional queries, localized
updates, temporal reasoning, and relation-aware planning that are
difficult to perform over independent, free-form text. These
capabilities, however, introduce substantial construction and
maintenance costs. Entities must be detected and resolved across
observations; attributes and relations must be extracted accurately;
schemas must accommodate previously unseen concepts; and updates must
maintain consistency as the environment evolves. Errors in entity
creation, relation extraction, or cross-observation data association may
propagate through retrieval, graph traversal, and downstream planning.
Structured representations therefore improve addressability and control
but do not inherently guarantee faithful memory content. Their
reliability depends on both accurately transforming perceptual evidence
into structured semantic content and correctly reconciling new evidence
with the existing graph by updating existing entities and relations or
introducing new ones.

### 3.3 Internalized Latent and Parametric Memory

While external memory preserves information as independently stored and
retrievable artifacts, such as raw observations, textual records,
structured entries, or modality-specific features, latent and parametric
memory integrate experience more directly into the model’s computation.
Latent memory maintains experience as continuous states that are carried
and updated during inference, whereas parametric memory internalizes
experience in model weights or dynamically generated adapters that shape
subsequent reasoning and action.

We distinguish two forms of memory that integrate experience directly
into model computation. Persistent multimodal latent states represent
experience as continuous vectors, memory tokens, hidden states, or
key–value units that are separate from backbone parameters. These states
can be updated during inference and integrated into the model through
attention, residual connections, or learned projection and fusion
modules. Recent systems apply this approach to retain visual information
and intermediate reasoning states ([Yu et al., 2026c](#bib.bib276)),
coordinate memory across visual agents ([Yu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib275)), and compress GUI interaction histories into
model-compatible continuous context ([Zhang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib281)). On the other hand, parametric internalization
encodes experience in model weights or experience-specific adapters.
Internalized memory influences subsequent inference implicitly, without
requiring retrieval or inclusion of the original multimodal evidence in
the input context. For example, Frames2LoRA ([Suri et al.,
2026](#bib.bib200)) generates a LoRA adapter from a video, enabling the
adapted model to use information from that video without processing its
visual tokens again. Instead, MemVerse ([Liu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib133)) periodically distills selected knowledge from an
explicit long-term memory store into a parametric memory model.

Both forms provide compact access to past experience and integrate
memory closely with the model’s reasoning and control processes. They
can reduce repeated encoding, retrieval costs, and context growth while
retaining information that may be difficult to capture in language or
symbolic structures. This close integration, however, limits direct
control over the stored information. Latent and parametric memories are
generally more difficult to inspect, edit, trace to specific
observations, or transfer across models with incompatible architectures.
Latent compression may discard information that cannot be recovered,
while repeated parameter updates may cause interference or forgetting.

#### 3.3.1 Persistent Multimodal Latent State

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Common implementations use hidden states ([Qian et al.,
2024](#bib.bib168)), memory tokens ([Wang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib227)),
or key–value caches ([Xiao et al., 2026b](#bib.bib250)) and integrate
them with the current input through attention, residual connections, or
learned projection and fusion layers.

KV caches can also serve as persistent latent memory when they are
deliberately retained and reused beyond the computation that produced
them. ReKV, for example, incrementally constructs and retains
video-derived KV states and selectively restores query-relevant blocks
for later question answering ([Di et al., 2025](#bib.bib37)). MuKV
further compresses multi-grained KV states to support long-horizon
streaming video question answering under bounded memory ([Xiao et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib250)).

Shared and recurrent latent states have been widely explored in
image-based agents to preserve visual information and intermediate
reasoning across inference steps. VisMem ([Yu et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib276)) uses a short-term memory former to generate latent
tokens containing fine-grained evidence from the current visual input,
and a long-term memory former provides higher-level semantic knowledge
relevant to the current reasoning context. The model learns when to
invoke each memory type and inserts the resulting latent tokens into the
inference sequence. TRAM ([Liu et al., 2026h](#bib.bib134)) preserves
information from earlier reasoning steps so that it can inform later
stages of a multi-step reasoning process. After each reasoning step, the
model summarizes its internal activations and uses them to update two
recurrent latent states with different decay rates. The fast state
emphasizes recently completed reasoning, while the slow state retains
information over a longer portion of the trajectory. Their combined
representation is then added to selected decoder layers at the beginning
of the next reasoning step. These methods address a common limitation of
extended multimodal reasoning: visual evidence and intermediate
conclusions may lose influence as the generation grows longer ([Wu et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib239)).

For long video streams, latent memory can reduce the cost of repeatedly
processing accumulated visual context ([Chen et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib22)). Light-Omni ([Nie et al., 2026b](#bib.bib161))
maintains a bounded, non-parametric global state by progressively
summarizing and merging episodic scripts. This hierarchical state
preserves recent events in greater detail while representing older
events through higher-level summaries. Given the global state and the
current multimodal input, the model generates latent features that
determine whether to speak or search and produce an embedding for
retrieving relevant entries from long-term memory. Light-Omni therefore
adopts a hybrid design: explicit episodic scripts and their consolidated
global state preserve historical information, while the generated latent
features support immediate action control and context-aware retrieval.
This design is well suited to long-video tasks, which require both a
compact representation of global context and access to specific events,
temporal details, or original multimodal evidence.

Beyond modality-specific designs for images and video, latent memory can
also support information sharing among multiple vision-language agents.
L²-VMAS ([Yu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib275)) maintains two shared memory
banks: a perception memory that stores latent representations of visual
inputs and a thinking memory that stores hidden states from previous
agents’ reasoning. Both are organized as key-value memory units that can
be retrieved and integrated into subsequent agent computation.

GUI agents use latent memory to connect interaction history with the
current interface state ([Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib242)). Mem-W ([Zhang
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib281)) uses a shared trajectory-to-latent
compressor to encode two sources of GUI memory: completed trajectories
retrieved from an external memory bank and the expired prefix of the
current interaction. The resulting memory tokens are combined with the
task instruction, current screenshot, and recent observation-action
context in a unified continuous embedding sequence. Retrieved
trajectories provide procedural evidence from both successful and failed
experiences, while the compressed in-session history preserves
unfinished task progress. Both forms of experience can therefore
directly inform the agent’s next action without being converted into
textual summaries. This representation is well suited to GUI tasks,
where the relevant state is distributed across visual observations,
previous actions, and intermediate task progress.

This approach extends naturally from GUI interaction to embodied
control, where agents must relate current observations to previous
actions and task progress ([Li et al., 2026j](#bib.bib114)). LaMem-VLA
([Qu et al., 2026](#bib.bib172)) organizes an agent’s interaction
history into two complementary memory vaults: a short-term vault that
retains recent visual information and a long-term vault that preserves
task progress and action continuity. Given the current observation and
instruction, the model retrieves relevant information from both vaults
and compresses it into fixed-length latent memory tokens. These tokens
are combined with the current visual, instruction, and action-query
tokens in a unified embedding sequence, allowing historical experience
to directly guide action generation . This design is well suited to
Vision-Language-Action (VLAs) models because it integrates perception,
memory, and control within a shared continuous representation space.

Persistent latent memory remains relatively underexplored in audio and
speech agents. These systems more commonly preserve semantic content as
transcripts ([Jiang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib86)) and represent speaker
identity, prosody, and other acoustic properties as separately
accessible features ([Someki et al., 2026](#bib.bib189)). Such
representations support direct retrieval and speaker attribution while
retaining temporal and acoustic evidence that recurrent compression may
discard. Consequently, persistent latent states designed to preserve
general auditory experience across long interactions or multiple
episodes remain less developed than their counterparts in visual
reasoning, GUI interaction, and embodied control.

Across modalities, latent memory operates over different persistence
horizons. Some latent states are maintained within a single reasoning
trajectory ([Yu et al., 2026c](#bib.bib276); [Liu et al.,
2026h](#bib.bib134)), whereas others preserve information across
successive agents or interaction steps ([Yu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib275);
[Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib281)). Latent representations may also be
constructed on demand from retrieved long-term experience ([Zhang et
al., 2026b](#bib.bib281); [Qu et al., 2026](#bib.bib172)). Despite these
differences, these mechanisms share a common property: past experience
is represented in a continuous form that directly contributes to
subsequent model computation.

#### 3.3.2 Experience-Conditioned Parametric Memory

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A system may update shared model parameters through gradient-based
learning ([Lin et al., 2026e](#bib.bib125)) or encode experience in
instance- or task-specific adapters attached to a frozen backbone ([Wang
et al., 2026d](#bib.bib217); [Wang et al., 2026k](#bib.bib224)). Once
encoded in shared weights or a selected adapter, the information
influences model computation without retrieving the original
observations or adding them to the input context.

Image-based parametric memory has primarily been explored through
multimodal knowledge editing, where the objective is to retain newly
introduced or corrected visual facts within a model. MemEIC ([Seong et
al., 2025](#bib.bib180)) adopts a hybrid design that combines explicit
evidence with parametric internalization. It maintains separate LoRA
adapters for visual and textual knowledge updates while keeping the
pretrained backbone frozen. A visual edit updates only the visual
adapter, whereas a textual edit updates only the textual adapter. During
inference, the system activates the adapter associated with the query
modality; when a query requires both modalities, it activates both
adapters and uses a learned connector to combine their representations.
This design illustrates both an advantage and a challenge of parametric
memory. Incorporating an edit into learned parameters allows the updated
knowledge to participate directly in subsequent computation, but
repeatedly writing heterogeneous information into shared parameters can
cause interference and forgetting. MemEIC addresses this problem by
separating parameter updates by modality, while retaining explicit edit
records externally for reliable retrieval and verification.

Video introduces a different motivation for parametric memory:
supporting repeated queries without retaining and reprocessing a long
sequence of visual tokens. Frames2LoRA ([Suri et al.,
2026](#bib.bib200)) first encodes a video using a frozen vision-language
model. A Perceiver-based hypernetwork then converts the resulting
layer-wise representations into a video-specific LoRA adapter in a
single forward pass. This adapter is attached to the frozen model and
acts as a reusable parametric representation of the video. For each
subsequent question, the model receives only the textual query, while
information from the video influences its response through the adapter
parameters; neither the original video nor its visual tokens are
included in the input context. Unlike conventional per-video
fine-tuning, the method does not iteratively optimize a new adapter for
each video. Instead, its trained hypernetwork directly generates the
adapter from the video representations. Frames2LoRA therefore
demonstrates how parametric memory can convert a particular video into a
compact and reusable parameter component, reducing the cost of repeated
inference while sacrificing direct access to the original visual
evidence.

In GUI agents, parametric memory more commonly captures reusable
operational knowledge than the appearance of a particular screen ([Jin
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib89); [Lin et al., 2026e](#bib.bib125)). SE-GA
([Jin et al., 2026b](#bib.bib89)) illustrates this form of experience
internalization through a hybrid memory architecture. During task
execution, its Test-Time Memory Extension component maintains an
explicit repository containing current task state, general GUI rules,
and successful trajectories from previous tasks. Its Memory-Augmented
Self-Evolution pipeline subsequently uses the accumulated interaction
data to improve the agent’s policy through grounding supervision and
reinforcement learning, with parameter-efficient LoRA updates used
