during self-evolution. The explicit repository makes recent and
task-specific experience immediately retrievable, whereas the learned
policy parameters absorb recurring interaction patterns so that they can
influence future actions without replaying every source trajectory.
SE-GA therefore exemplifies a slower form of parametric consolidation in
which accumulated GUI experience is converted into a more general action
policy. Fully parametric, episode-specific GUI memory remains uncommon
because successful interaction often depends on exact screenshots,
interface states, and action histories that are easier to inspect,
revise, and reuse when retained explicitly.

Embodied control provides a clear example of parametric memory stored in
separate, reusable adapters. Rather than merging all experience into the
model’s shared weights, VLA-Pro ([Si et al., 2026](#bib.bib188))
maintains task-specific LoRA adapters that can be retrieved and combined
according to the current situation. VLA-Pro first trains a shared LoRA
adapter across previously seen manipulation tasks and then learns a
separate task-specific adapter for each task. Each memory entry pairs
its adapter with a sequence of structured procedural states describing
when the stored behavior is relevant. These states specify the action
type, object geometry, end-effector orientation, and target interaction
point. Given the current visual observation, language instruction, and
interaction history, the system extracts the agent’s current procedural
state and retrieves the most relevant task memories. It then combines
their LoRA adapters using similarity-based weights, temporarily attaches
the fused adapter to the vision-language-action model, and uses the
adapted policy to generate the next action chunk. VLA-Pro demonstrates
that parametric memory need not be incorporated permanently into a
single set of shared weights. Parameterized experiences can instead
remain modular, indexed by explicit descriptors, and selectively
composed according to the current situation. This organization achieves
a milestone improvement in cross-task transfer while limiting
interference from unrelated manipulation behaviors.

Together, these systems show that parametric memory can operate at
different granularities and persistence horizons. MemEIC ([Seong et al.,
2025](#bib.bib180)) accumulates modality-specific knowledge edits,
Frames2LoRA ([Suri et al., 2026](#bib.bib200)) generates a separate
adapter for each video, SE-GA ([Jin et al., 2026b](#bib.bib89))
consolidates interaction experience into a shared GUI policy, and
VLA-Pro ([Si et al., 2026](#bib.bib188)) stores task-specific action
adapters that can be retrieved and composed. Their common property is
that past information influences later computation through learned
parameters rather than solely through replayed observations or records.
Parametric memory can therefore reduce repeated context processing and
support direct behavioral adaptation, but it also makes the underlying
evidence less accessible and introduces challenges in updating,
attribution, interference control, and deletion. Consequently, many
multimodal agents combine parametric internalization with explicit
memory that preserves source evidence and provides more controllable
access.

### 3.4 Hybrid Representations

The preceding subsections describe three primary forms of multimodal
memory: source- and modality-specific evidence, textual and structured
records, and latent or parametric representations. Each form offers
different advantages. Source evidence preserves perceptual detail,
textual and structured records support efficient retrieval and explicit
reasoning, and latent or parametric representations can contribute
directly to model computation. In practice, however, no single form is
sufficient for every memory operation. Hybrid memory is not an
additional elementary encoding type; rather, it describes how different
representations are organized and used together within a memory system.
An important subtype is _source-linked memory_, in which an abstract
record retains a reference to the original observation or to selected
evidence preserved from it. The agent can then search and reason over
compact abstractions while recovering the corresponding image, frame,
audio segment, or interface region when finer perceptual evidence is
required.

For collections of images and visually rich documents, hybrid
representations allow an agent to organize large amounts of retrieved
evidence without reducing all visual content to text ([Wang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib209)). VimRAG ([Wang et al., 2026e](#bib.bib218))
represents iterative multimodal retrieval and reasoning as a directed
acyclic graph. Each node records its dependencies on earlier nodes, the
subquery that produced it, a concise textual summary, and a multimodal
memory bank containing visual tokens from retrieved images or video
frames. The graph exposes the temporal and logical structure of the
reasoning process, while the visual tokens preserve information that may
be lost in textual summarization. To operate under a bounded context
budget, VimRAG dynamically adjusts the number of visual tokens retained
for each memory item according to its semantic relevance, recency, and
position in the reasoning graph. The method therefore demonstrates a
combined hybrid representation: structured and textual components
organize the agent’s reasoning state, whereas continuous visual
representations preserve perceptual information for later verification
and answer generation.

Video streams create a stronger need to connect compact semantic records
with recoverable visual evidence because relevant events may occur far
apart, and details omitted during summarization may become important
only after a query is received. FOLIO ([Fan et al., 2026a](#bib.bib42))
combines a short-term buffer of recent frames, a long-term semantic
memory, and a visual-evidence cache. As the video arrives, the system
constructs structured records describing entities, attributes,
locations, relations, actions, and state changes. These records contain
timestamps and references to selected keyframes retained in the evidence
cache. At query time, FOLIO retrieves relevant semantic records and can
restore their associated keyframes when additional visual grounding is
needed. The structured memory supports efficient long-horizon access,
while the linked frames preserve visual details that the records may
omit or describe incorrectly. FOLIO thus exemplifies source-linked
hybrid memory: semantic abstraction reduces the cost of storing and
searching a long video, but it does not permanently replace the
observations from which the memory was derived.

In GUI interaction, source linkage is useful because a textual
description may capture the meaning of an earlier interface event while
omitting the precise visual target or interface state needed for a later
action. MementoGUI ([Zeng et al., 2026](#bib.bib278)) maintains both
within-episode working memory and cross-episode episodic memory. For a
selected interaction step, a working-memory entry contains a textual
event summary, the bounding box of the relevant interface region, a crop
of that region, and a visual embedding used only to organize the memory.
When older entries are compressed, their textual content is summarized,
but identifiers for selected visual regions are retained and later
resolved back into the corresponding crops. Episodic-memory entries
similarly combine trajectory summaries and action metadata with
representative interface crops and retrieval embeddings. During action
generation, the agent receives the retrieved textual summaries and
region-of-interest images through the frozen GUI model’s standard
multimodal input interface. MementoGUI therefore represents interface
experience through source-linked textual and visual components: text
records task progress and the significance of earlier events, while
linked crops recover localized details such as icons, labels, selected
values, and interface states. Its retrieval embeddings serve only as
indices and do not themselves constitute the memory records to be
retrieved and used.

In interactive visual environments, hybrid memory can combine a
continuously revised semantic state with a complete record of visual
interaction, since details that appear unimportant at one step may
become useful later. VISTA ([Han et al., 2026](#bib.bib60)) maintains
two forms of memory in parallel: revisable textual notes that summarize
reusable environment knowledge and the agent’s current state, and a
lossless visual memory that stores every returned frame in its original
form. During reasoning, the agent can rely on the compact textual state
for routine planning while selectively revisiting arbitrary past frames
or spatial regions when finer-grained perceptual evidence is needed.
Unlike source-linked designs in which individual abstract records
explicitly reference particular observations, VISTA keeps its textual
state and visual history separately addressable and combines them on
demand.

Embodied agents require hybrid memory to preserve perceptual evidence
while organizing it according to the spatial structure of the
environment ([Li et al., 2026e](#bib.bib109)). ObsGraph ([Lee et al.,
2026](#bib.bib99)) constructs an observation-centered hierarchical scene
graph with room, view, and object layers. Room-level representations
provide coarse semantic anchors, view-level memories preserve
observations in which multiple objects appear together, and object-level
memories retain fine-grained visual information about individual
objects. Relations among these layers connect object evidence to the
views and rooms in which it was observed. Given a task, the agent
retrieves memory progressively from rooms to views and objects under a
bounded budget. The level at which relevant evidence is missing also
determines whether the agent should search another room, refine an
existing viewpoint, or explore an unobserved frontier. ObsGraph
therefore combines semantic hierarchy, spatial structure, and retained
visual observations. The structured graph supports efficient retrieval
and planning, while its linked visual evidence preserves appearance and
co-visibility information that semantic labels alone cannot express.
This combination is particularly important in embodied settings because
memory must support not only retrospective question answering but also
decisions about where to move and what additional evidence to acquire.
Beyond navigation, HiMe ([Ji et al., 2026](#bib.bib81)) addresses
long-horizon manipulation with a hierarchical hybrid-memory architecture
that combines recent visual working memory, image–text contextual
records, and a structured procedural plan to retain evolving object
states and task progress across action sequences.

Across modalities, hybrid representations exploit the strengths of
different memory forms. Textual and structured records provide compact
semantic access, explicit relations, and controllable updates, whereas
retained observations and modality-specific representations preserve
perceptual detail and the provenance of abstracted information. Their
combination enables a tiered access strategy: agents can rely on compact
abstractions for routine retrieval and reasoning, while selectively
recovering higher-fidelity evidence when a task requires verification,
reinterpretation, or details lost during abstraction. This capability is
likely to become increasingly important as multimodal agents operate
over longer histories and in dynamic environments, where retaining all
observations in the active context is impractical but irreversible
compression is unreliable. Hybrid memory may therefore emerge as a
prominent design pattern, particularly for applications in which both
efficiency and evidential grounding are important. Its effectiveness,
however, depends on more than storing multiple representations. Systems
must preserve valid links as memories are revised, merged, or removed;
maintain consistency between abstract records and their supporting
observations; and learn when compact memory is sufficient and when
source evidence should be restored. The central challenge is thus to
coordinate representations of different fidelity, cost, and
accessibility so that an agent can move between efficient abstraction
and grounded perceptual recall as its information needs change.

## 4 Axis II: Memory Management

![Refer to caption](2610.19366v1/memory-management-progression.png)

Figure 7: Progression across the three memory-management tiers. T1
Static Memory stores and reuses fixed memory. T2 Dynamic Memory updates
memory through a stable policy. T3 Self-Evolving Memory updates memory
through an evolving policy. The tiers therefore represent an increasing
scope of change, from memory access to memory-state updates and,
finally, policy evolution.

After forming memory records from raw messages, experience, and related
metadata, the memory system must control how these representations are
maintained, accessed, and changed as experience accumulates.
[Figure 7](#S4.F7 "In 4 Axis II: Memory Management ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
summarizes this progression from T1 Static Memory to T2 Dynamic Memory
and T3 Self-Evolving Memory. Specifically, memory management operations
include writing, updating, consolidation, reorganization, retention, and
forgetting, while retrieval selects relevant memory for ongoing
reasoning and action. These operation mechanisms may be governed by
heuristic rules ([Yang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib265)), fixed prompts ([Ali
et al., 2025](#bib.bib5)), frozen learned modules ([Li et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib104)), optimization procedures ([Wang et al.,
2026m](#bib.bib230)), or policies that themselves adapt from deployment
feedback ([Zou et al., 2026a](#bib.bib297)).

Multimodal memory introduces another representational challenge compared
to textual inputs. Multimodal inputs are often high-dimensional and
expensive to retain in their original form. Therefore, systems must
balance storage and retrieval efficiency against the ability to recover
source evidence, leading to the diverse representation choices discussed
in Axis I. Hybrid systems may preserve multiple representations to
balance information fidelity and computational efficiency. Consequently,
multimodal memory management involves not only updating memory content
but also maintaining consistency across these linked representations. It
must determine which representations should change, how updates should
propagate among related representations, and whether abstracted memories
remain valid and grounded in their source evidence as experience
accumulates. Conceptually, we can model these representations as nodes
in a representation graph connected by transformation, alignment,
fusion, and grounding relations. Memory operations then act on both the
representation states and the relations connecting them. We distinguish
three tiers according to what can change during inference.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The distinction between memory-state updates and policy evolution
depends on the function of the updated component. Memory state includes
stored content, organization, access indices, and descriptive metadata,
while the management policy governs how memory operations are selected
and performed. Changes to retrieval keys, skill descriptions, or usage
statistics can alter subsequent retrieval results without changing this
policy. Such changes should remain within T2 Dynamic Memory when the
selection and update mechanisms remain stable. T3 Self-Evolving Memory
goes beyond state modification by using feedback to persistently revise
reusable management rules, instructions, procedures, or learned policy
components.

Accordingly, the three tiers distinguish whether the memory state and
the policy that manages it change during inference. Axis II, _Memory
Management_, organizes systems by the scope of persistent
deployment-time change they support. Across these tiers, multimodal
information may remain within one representation, be projected into
another representation, be fused across multiple modalities, or be
jointly maintained across linked representations. The tiers therefore
progress from reusing fixed memory, to updating memory through a stable
policy, and finally to updating memory through an evolving policy, while
the transition patterns characterize how multimodal information moves
through the representation system. Updating memory state and evolving
management policies can help agents adapt to changing environments and
mitigate training–deployment mismatch, but these changes may also
introduce instability and make memory updates harder to control. The
following subsections examine memory access and reuse in T1 Static
Memory, five memory-state operations in T2 Dynamic Memory, and the
evolution of writing, maintenance, and retrieval policies in T3
Self-Evolving Memory.

### 4.1 T1: Static Memory

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

T1 Static Memory is well suited to large, static corpora ([Yu et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib274)), stable knowledge bases ([Yu et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib274); [Hu et al., 2023](#bib.bib71)), and invariant
environment or task information that must be retrieved and reused across
subsequent reasoning steps or tasks, such as long-video analysis ([Fan
et al., 2024](#bib.bib44)) or navigation with a preconstructed
environment map ([Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib72)). The absence of an
update policy preserves the memory state across tasks and prevents
unverified outputs from modifying it. Representative systems across
modalities follow this pattern by constructing memory before downstream
task execution and leaving it unchanged during subsequent use ([Zhang et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib280); [Zhang et al., 2025d](#bib.bib285); [Li et
al., 2026d](#bib.bib108)).

Because T1 Static Memory undergoes a single formation cycle, its stored
representations and their relationships remain unchanged after
formation. Subsequent access and retrieval operations neither modify nor
reorganize the persistent memory. Accordingly, the principal design
variables in T1 Static Memory systems are the indexing and retrieval
mechanisms, which may be optimized during system development or memory
formation but remain fixed during inference. Fixed multimodal memories
may be organized as flat sequential records ([Wu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib241)), vector-indexed collections ([Wang et al.,
2026g](#bib.bib220)), hierarchical or multi-tier ([Wang et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib216)), relational graphs ([Su et al.,
2026](#bib.bib194)), inference-time latent states ([Wu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib242)), or parametric modules ([Si et al.,
2026](#bib.bib188)). Retrieval-augmented generation provides a common
access framework for vector-indexed memory, using dense cross-modal
similarity, late interaction, or reranking to retrieve relevant images,
document pages, video segments, audio spans, or cross-represented
textual records ([Yu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib274); [Wang et al.,
2026j](#bib.bib223); [Yeo et al., 2026a](#bib.bib268); [Fan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib44)). Metadata-aware and spatiotemporal retrieval further
exploits timestamps, locations, speaker identities, and temporal
boundaries to localize relevant experiences, sometimes through
hierarchical coarse-to-fine search ([Jiang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib84);
[Someki et al., 2026](#bib.bib189)). Relational memories support
explicit traversal over connections among objects, states, events, or
interface transitions ([Shen et al., 2025](#bib.bib182); [Wen et al.,
2024](#bib.bib235); [Yu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib273)). Planner- or
tool-assisted retrieval decomposes a query and routes its subqueries to
modality-specific indexes, temporal search tools, or structured
databases ([Fan et al., 2024](#bib.bib44); [Someki et al.,
2026](#bib.bib189)). Inference-time latent-state and parametric memory
systems are less common in this setting because their stored information
is less explicit and interpretable ([Suri et al., 2026](#bib.bib200)).

In practice, static memory supports three main types of downstream
applications: static knowledge bases, reusable evidence or environment
stores, and reusable procedural knowledge. First, it can retain external
knowledge or documentation for domain-specific applications, such as
medicine, thereby improving grounding and reducing hallucinations ([Xia
et al., 2025](#bib.bib246)). Second, it can store expensive-to-process
but largely static content, such as long videos ([Fan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib44)) or GUI environments ([Wen et al.,
2024](#bib.bib235)), through one-time ingestion and reuse this
information across subsequent tasks ([Fan et al., 2024](#bib.bib44);
[Wen et al., 2024](#bib.bib235)). Finally, static memory can preserve
procedural knowledge for repeated action planning and execution ([Si et
al., 2026](#bib.bib188)).

T1 Static Memory is most effective when the underlying information
changes slowly and the stored representation will be reused across
tasks. Expensive operations such as document encoding, video analysis,
environment exploration, and adapter training are performed during
memory formation. Because the stored content remains unchanged, each
task accesses the same evidence, environment model, or procedural
library. This stability supports consistent behavior.

However, this stability limits the system’s ability to respond to
change. T1 Static Memory preserves both the useful information and any
omissions or errors introduced during its formation. During normal task
execution, it cannot incorporate corrections to stored evidence, changes
in an interface or physical environment, or procedural knowledge gained
from later successes and failures. The stored representation may
therefore become incomplete or outdated as the source, environment, or
task distribution changes.

### 4.2 T2: Dynamic Memory

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

We organize T2 Dynamic Memory methods around five fundamental memory
operations.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In multimodal memory systems, the central design challenge is to perform
these operations across heterogeneous representations while preserving
relevant information and cross-modal relationships. Therefore, to
systematically examine T2 Dynamic Memory methods, we characterize each
fundamental memory operation along two multimodal-specific dimensions.
The representation-handling pattern indicates whether an operation acts
locally within a single representation, coordinates distinct
representations while keeping them separable, or transforms information
across representations through projection or fusion. The computational
mechanism specifies how the resulting memory change is produced: through
hard-coded heuristics, a prompted LLM, a trained functional update
module, or iterative optimization under a fixed objective.

#### 4.2.1 Memory Update

Memory update incorporates new observations, interactions, or feedback
into persistent memory. Depending on the target representation, an
update may append new evidence, revise an existing record, modify a
structured state, integrate information into a latent state, or edit
specific model parameters. The central multimodal challenge is to
incorporate new information while preserving existing content in
abstract representations, cross-modal alignment, and relationships among
linked representations.

Source-preserving memories incorporate new information by inserting
observations, replacing outdated evidence, or modifying associated
metadata. Source-preserving memories commonly incorporate new
information by appending raw or minimally processed multimodal
observations to an evidence log or feature buffer, thereby retaining
prior perceptual evidence without rewriting it ([Diko et al.,
2025](#bib.bib38); [Feng et al., 2026](#bib.bib46)). The appended
evidence may include metadata, source links, or derived retrieval
indices that support efficient access while preserving the original
observations ([Feng et al., 2026](#bib.bib46)).

Modality-specific feature representations are generally updated through
within-modality matching followed by feature aggregation or insertion.
Each incoming feature is compared with stored representations from the
same modality. If a match is identified, the corresponding memory entry
is augmented, averaged, or replaced; otherwise, a new entry is created.
This mechanism preserves modality-specific evidence while using shared
entity identifiers to coordinate related information across modalities
([Long et al., 2026](#bib.bib143)).

Geometric memory representations are updated by first registering new
observations within a common spatial reference frame and then
associating the projected measurements or detected instances with
existing spatial elements. Matched elements may be updated through
feature fusion or attribute modification, whereas unmatched observations
may create new map cells, objects, nodes, or relations. Invalid or
obsolete elements may likewise be removed ([Liu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib135); [Jiang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib83); [Mitash et al.,
2020](#bib.bib153)). These predefined association and fusion procedures
provide explicit control over spatial updates and help preserve
geometric consistency, but their reliability depends on fixed matching
criteria and their robustness to noisy, incomplete, or conflicting
observations.

Structured memory representations organize information as entities,
relations, events, or procedures. New information is incorporated by
identifying the relevant structural unit and then modifying its
attributes, inserting or removing nodes and edges, adjusting relation
weights, or updating transition statistics. Target units may be selected
through similarity-based gating, while their indices and relations are
maintained through moving-average aggregation, count updates, and
graph-editing operators ([Jiang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib85)).

Textual semantic records derived from multimodal experience retain
perceptual or interaction information as natural-language facts,
attributes, or event descriptions. Unlike structured memories, whose
updates modify explicit entities, relations, or topology, these records
are maintained through content-level semantic edits. Updating them
requires interpreting incoming evidence relative to existing content and
selecting an operation such as addition, modification, confirmation,
deletion, or no change. Prompted LLMs or VLMs are used to perform this
comparison because the system must determine whether new evidence
confirms, extends, contradicts, or supersedes an existing record from
the multimodal experience ([Feng et al., 2026](#bib.bib46); [Hong et
al., 2026](#bib.bib67); [Ma et al., 2026](#bib.bib148); [Ji et al.,
2026](#bib.bib81)).

Latent memory incorporates new information through trained parameterized
modules that either transform an existing latent state or construct new
latent memory entries. Recurrent state-transition modules integrate the
preceding latent state with the current multimodal representation to
produce a successor state ([Qian et al., 2024](#bib.bib168)).
Query-based write modules instead distill incoming features,
instructions, and retrieved context into compact tokens that are added
to a latent memory bank ([Diko et al., 2025](#bib.bib38)). Thus, the
former modifies an existing latent representation, whereas the latter
expands the memory with newly constructed latent entries. Because both
forms distribute information across latent vectors, their updates are
generally difficult to inspect, attribute to specific observations, or
correct selectively.

Parametric memory incorporates new information by routing it to a
designated subset of model parameters and optimizing those parameters
under a fixed editing objective ([Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib133)).
Modality-specific adapters can restrict visual and textual edits to
separate parameter subsets, limiting interference across modalities and
unrelated model behavior ([Seong et al., 2025](#bib.bib180)). Unlike a
trained functional module, which computes the next memory state through
a forward pass, a parametric editor produces the updated memory through
inference-time optimization. The central challenge is to internalize new
information while preserving previously stored knowledge and maintaining
the model’s behavior on unrelated inputs.

Hybrid memory systems coordinate updates across multiple
representational forms, such as source evidence, semantic records,
latent tokens, and model parameters. Common mechanisms include linking
editable semantic records to immutable source evidence ([Feng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib46)), maintaining compact latent representations alongside
detailed perceptual features ([Diko et al., 2025](#bib.bib38)), and
coupling parametric edits with corresponding external records ([Seong et
al., 2025](#bib.bib180)). These coordinated pathways preserve the
complementary properties and provenance of different representations.
However, they must keep linked memory components consistent as new
information is incorporated, without collapsing representational
distinctions or breaking associations.

#### 4.2.2 Memory Consolidation

Memory consolidation transforms related stored information into a less
redundant, more compact representation. Unlike update, which
incorporates an incoming experience, consolidation operates across
accumulated memories. Its central multimodal challenge is to reduce
storage and retrieval costs without removing perceptual details,
temporal distinctions, modality-specific evidence, or
cross-representation links that may remain important for later
reasoning. Existing mechanisms primarily perform feature-space
compression, semantic abstraction, structured merging, or coordinated
consolidation across representations ([Lian et al., 2026](#bib.bib118)).

Feature-space compression reduces redundancy among stored perceptual or
latent encodings. Temporally adjacent or semantically similar visual
features can be selected through fixed similarity criteria and then
averaged ([He et al., 2024](#bib.bib61)), clustered ([Zhang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib282)), or merged ([Song et al., 2026](#bib.bib191)) into
a smaller set of representative tokens. More adaptive mechanisms vary
the degree of compression according to temporal change or semantic
salience, preserving more features around distinctive events while
compressing repetitive observations more aggressively ([Song et al.,
2024](#bib.bib190); [Fan et al., 2026a](#bib.bib42); [Wang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib226)). FluxMem ([Xie et al., 2026b](#bib.bib253)), for
example, achieves competitive performance by retaining recent
observations at full resolution, removing temporally redundant tokens
from mid-term memory, and further consolidating spatially repetitive
regions in long-term memory. These mechanisms bound memory growth, but
overly aggressive compression may remove brief actions, fine visual
details, or temporal transitions that cannot be recovered from the
consolidated features.

Semantic abstraction can likewise consolidate a growing video history in
language space. ReMA ([Chen et al., 2026a](#bib.bib20)) first appends
timestamp-aligned descriptions for successive video clips. Whenever a
new passive or query-directed observation overlaps existing temporal
nodes, a prompted summarizer merges the old and new content and replaces
those nodes with a unified record; non-overlapping observations are
added as new entries. The same procedure operates during initial stream
ingestion and recursive query answering, so the belief state continues
to change while the memory-management policy remains stable. ReMA
therefore exemplifies consolidation in T2 Dynamic Memory rather than
policy evolution in T3 Self-Evolving Memory: task-specific inspection
can refine what is stored, but task outcomes do not update the rule
governing later memory operations.

Structured merging consolidates memories whose internal organization
must be preserved. Graph alignment and matching procedures identify
equivalent entities, actions, or procedural steps before merging their
nodes, edges, alternative paths, and associated statistics ([Yeo et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib269)). Recurring action sequences may also be extracted
from multiple episodes and converted into reusable procedural structures
([Jiang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib85)). Unlike feature averaging,
structured merging must determine which elements are genuinely
equivalent and which represent meaningful alternatives; incorrect
alignment can collapse distinct entities, actions, or execution paths.

Coordinated cross-representation consolidation creates a compact
representation while retaining links to complementary forms of evidence.
A visual sequence may be compressed into representative features and
paired with a textual clue ([Xiong et al., 2025](#bib.bib255)), an
audiovisual episode may be summarized while preserving timestamps and
representative frames ([Yan et al., 2026](#bib.bib261)), or an
entity-level fact may remain linked to the observations from which it
was derived ([Ma et al., 2026](#bib.bib148)). This coordination allows
the compact memory to support efficient retrieval while the linked
source or lower-level representation preserves details omitted during
abstraction. The central requirement is therefore not to preserve every
representation at equal resolution, but to maintain sufficient links for
the consolidated memory to be interpreted, verified, or expanded when
needed.

#### 4.2.3 Memory Revision

Memory revision corrects an existing memory when new evidence indicates
that its content is inaccurate, inconsistent, incomplete, or outdated.
The revision operation is narrower than update: adding an independent
observation constitutes an update, whereas modifying or replacing an
existing record in response to conflicting or superseding evidence
constitutes revision. It also differs from forgetting, which removes
information because of capacity, recency, or importance rather than
because new experiences show the information to be incorrect. In
multimodal systems, revision primarily involves spatial and object-state
correction, semantic revision, and conflict reconciliation across linked
representations.

Spatial and object-state correction revises geometric or structured
environment memory when new observations indicate that an object has
moved, disappeared, changed state, or been incorrectly associated with
an existing entity. The mechanism registers each new observation within
a common spatial reference frame and identifies the affected object or
map region through geometric and semantic matching. It then replaces
outdated attributes, removes invalid entities, updates object geometry,
or recomputes spatial relations within the affected subgraph ([Jiang et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib83); [Yan et al., 2025b](#bib.bib262)). Restricting
revision to the affected region avoids reconstructing the entire
environment representation, but reliable correction requires maintaining
object identity despite occlusion, viewpoint changes, and noisy
observations.

Semantic revision operates on explicit facts, attributes, and event
records derived from multimodal experience. Incoming evidence is
compared with existing records to determine whether it confirms,
extends, contradicts, or supersedes their content. Prompted LLMs or VLMs
commonly perform this comparison and select among fixed operations such
as modification, replacement, deletion, confirmation, or no change
([Feng et al., 2026](#bib.bib46); [Hong et al., 2026](#bib.bib67); [Ma
et al., 2026](#bib.bib148); [Yeo et al., 2026b](#bib.bib269)). Effective
revision must correct outdated information without replacing compatible
records merely because the new observation is incomplete or expressed
differently.

Cross-representation conflict reconciliation is required when the same
experience is retained as source evidence and as one or more derived
semantic or structured records. Evidence identifiers or entity
associations can be used to retrieve the observations supporting a
disputed record before the record is revised. The correction is then
applied to the derived representation while its links to the supporting
visual, auditory, or interaction evidence are retained ([Feng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib46); [Ma et al., 2026](#bib.bib148)). This mechanism
preserves provenance and supports later verification, but it must
determine whether an apparent conflict reflects a genuine change, an
unreliable observation, or information that is valid only under a
different temporal or situational context.

#### 4.2.4 Memory Reorganization

Memory reorganization changes the structural role, placement, or access
path of information that remains in memory. It does not primarily add
observations, correct content, or combine multiple memories. Instead, it
determines where retained information resides and how it is connected or
retrieved. Multimodal memory systems primarily perform reorganization
through tier migration, graph relinking, and cross-representation
reindexing or association.

Tier migration transfers retained memory records between storages with
different temporal or functional roles, such as short- and long-term
memory or dynamic and static memory. A fixed trigger first identifies
information that meets a capacity, persistence, or stability criterion,
then moves or copies it to the appropriate destination. Compact visual
representations can be transferred from a bounded short-term buffer into
long-term memory ([Song et al., 2024](#bib.bib190)), while attributes
judged to be persistent can migrate from dynamic conversational state
into static personalized memory ([Hong et al., 2026](#bib.bib67)). Here,
tiers denote temporal or functional memory roles rather than hardware
storage levels. Moving an unchanged artifact between accelerator memory,
host memory, and storage is a physical residency decision, discussed in
[Sections 6.1](#S6.SS1 "6.1 Scope and System Abstractions ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
and [6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Physical Storage and Residency ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory");
it does not by itself reorganize the logical memory.

Graph relinking changes the relations through which retained entities or
events are structurally connected. When an embodied scene changes, links
involving affected objects can be invalidated and spatial relations
within the local subgraph recomputed without rebuilding the complete
scene representation ([Yan et al., 2025b](#bib.bib262)). Relinking can
also establish or reinforce associations between separately retained
modality-specific evidence, such as face and voice representations that
are determined to refer to the same persistent entity ([Long et al.,
2026](#bib.bib143)). These mechanisms support entity continuity and
cross-modal traversal, but incorrect associations can connect unrelated
evidence or propagate a local error through the graph.

Cross-representation reindexing changes the retrieval representation
associated with retained content without necessarily modifying the
underlying content or the retrieval policy. Incoming observations can be
compared with the goal- and step-level index vectors associated with an
existing procedural graph, after which the matched vectors are adjusted
through a fixed moving-average rule ([Jiang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib85)).
The procedure itself remains unchanged, but its retrieval keys can be
updated so that varied descriptions of the same task can reach a shared
procedural memory. More generally, reindexing and association
maintenance keep dense retrieval keys, modality-specific identifiers,
and structured memory items aligned as experience accumulates ([Zhu et
al., 2026c](#bib.bib296); [Yan et al., 2026](#bib.bib261)). Excessive
index drift or incorrect identity association, however, may make earlier
access paths unreliable.

#### 4.2.5 Memory Forgetting

Memory forgetting controls which accumulated information should remain
available to the agent and at what level of detail. The forgetting
operation may remove an item from an active store, reduce the detail
preserved in one representation, or lower a memory’s priority during
retrieval. In multimodal systems, forgetting need not affect every
representation of an experience equally: detailed perceptual evidence
may leave active memory while a compact event record, textual summary,
or linked long-term representation remains available. The major
mechanisms in the current literatures are active evidence eviction,
representation-detail decay, semantic accessibility decay, and
coordinated selective forgetting across linked representations.

Active evidence eviction removes source-preserving evidence or their
encodings from a bounded active memory. Selection may follow insertion
order such as first-in, first-out (FIFO), event-level reservoir
sampling, object identity, frequency and recency statistics, or
recency-weighted retention probabilities ([Lin et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib123); [Wen et al., 2026](#bib.bib236); [Wang et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib228); [Xiong et al., 2025](#bib.bib255)). Eviction bounds
active-memory cost, and removal from the active buffer does not imply
that all information derived from the observation has been erased from
long-term memory. They can be reorganized or migrated to another memory
store before being forgotten.

Representation-detail decay retains a memory in its source modality
while progressively reducing the detail or size of its representation.
Interaction histories rendered as memory images can be downsampled as
they recede in time, therefore reducing their resolution and
visual-token allocation while a more detailed textual record remains
available ([Li et al., 2026h](#bib.bib112)). Optical-forgetting
mechanisms similarly apply progressive resolution reduction to visually
represented memory pages, preserving coarse semantic structure while
discarding fine visual details ([Chang and Ren, 2026](#bib.bib18)).

Semantic accessibility decay preserves the content of an episodic or
semantic record while lowering its retrieval priority. A time-dependent
decay factor can reduce a record’s retrieval priority over time, while
repeated recall or contextual relevance may restore its priority ([Liu
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib133)). When retrieval priority decreases, the
memory remains stored but becomes less likely to enter the agent’s
working context. This mechanism provides more gradual control than
eviction, although an overly aggressive decay function may render stored
experiences effectively inaccessible.

Coordinated selective forgetting operates on experiences stored in
multiple representations and determines which representation should be
removed, compressed, or deprioritized while other representations are
retained. The goal is to exploit the complementary strengths of
different representations while reducing redundant storage. Detailed
visual information may be selectively discarded or compressed while a
more compact long-term representation is preserved ([Xiong et al.,
2025](#bib.bib255); [Li et al., 2026h](#bib.bib112); [Wang et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib228)).

### 4.3 T3: Self-Evolving Memory

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

T3 Self-Evolving Memory represents a memory-centered form of
inference-time learning in which experience accumulated during inference
drives improvements in memory management policies. Memory therefore
supports inference-time learning at two levels: accumulated experience
supports the agent’s inference-time learning, while the memory system
itself can also evolve through feedback-driven updates to its management
policies.

The evolving policy may be realized through learned parameters ([Zou et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib297)), symbolic rules ([Bärmann et al.,
2026](#bib.bib11)), utility-based decision criteria ([Sun et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib196)), or explicit procedures such as reusable retrieval
strategies ([Fan et al., 2026b](#bib.bib43)) and executable programs
([El Hattami et al., 2026](#bib.bib41)).

For multimodal memory, policy evolution must account for the different
roles of heterogeneous representations. A write policy determines which
source observations or features should be retained and how they should
be transformed into persistent records. A maintenance policy determines
which representations and levels of detail should remain available as
memory accumulates. A retrieval policy determines which representation
or store should be searched and how evidence across representations
should be coordinated. We therefore organize T3 Self-Evolving Memory
methods into writing-policy, maintenance-policy, and retrieval-policy
evolution.

#### 4.3.1 Write-Policy Evolution

Write-policy evolution uses feedback to improve how raw experiences are
selected and transformed into memory. Unlike a fixed write mechanism,
which repeatedly applies the same admission and
representation-transformation procedures, an evolving write policy
adapts what information is retained and how that information is
represented in response to feedback obtained during deployment.

The selection policy determines which parts of raw experience should be
retained as memory records. Feedback from new interactions or completed
tasks is used to adapt the policy toward retaining the most relevant
parts of raw experience that are likely to support subsequent reasoning
([Zou et al., 2026a](#bib.bib297)). However, this adaptation introduces
a key trade-off: when the task or environment changes substantially
during deployment, a policy optimized for prior experience may discard
important information in the new setting.

The transformation policy changes how selected multimodal evidence is
converted into the target memory representation. This evolution
currently operates through three main mechanisms. Representational
abstraction determines the semantic granularity and level of detail
preserved when raw experience is converted into an explicit record.
Normalization and grounding improve temporal alignment, entity
resolution, and contextual grounding across modality-specific
observations before they are committed to memory. Structural
construction changes how grounded evidence is organized into entities,
events, attributes, relations, or graph structures. In source-linked
memory, it may also adapt how derived semantic or structured records are
connected to their supporting visual observations, interaction traces,
timestamps, and entity identifiers. Failure traces can produce validated
policy changes that repair graph construction and source-to-record
mappings while preserving provenance and consistency across linked
representations ([Tian et al., 2026](#bib.bib205)). Across these
mechanisms, the central tension is to improve task relevance and
representational efficiency without losing source-grounded details,
temporal consistency, or cross-modal relationships needed by future
tasks.

#### 4.3.2 Maintenance-Policy Evolution

Maintenance-policy evolution uses feedback to improve how existing
memory representations are retained, revised, and removed over time. The
maintenance policy determines which stored representations persist and
how much information is preserved during operations such as
consolidation, reorganization, and forgetting. Unlike a fixed
maintenance policy, an evolving policy adapts these decisions based on
user feedback or accumulated evidence of downstream utility. Two main
mechanisms emerge for maintenance-policy evolution.

Feedback-driven retention uses user feedback to revise which memory
representations should remain available over time. When a failed memory
query reveals that relevant information was previously removed, the
feedback updates the retention policy so that similar information
encountered in the future is retained longer ([Bärmann et al.,
2026](#bib.bib11)). This mechanism improves future retention decisions
but cannot recover information already removed unless it remains
available through another linked representation. Feedback-driven
representation abstraction uses feedback to determine the information to
be preserved when a memory representation is being compressed. Updated
relevance criteria guide subsequent grouping and summarization toward
preserving information that has proved useful to the user or downstream
tasks.

#### 4.3.3 Retrieval-Policy Evolution

Retrieval-policy evolution uses feedback to improve the reusable
strategies that govern memory access. Specifically, the retrieval policy
determines how queries are formulated and how candidate memories are
prioritized for subsequent reasoning. Existing methods primarily focus
on two policy targets: search formulation and control, and memory
selection and prioritization.

Search formulation and control adapt how queries are constructed and how
incomplete retrieval is repaired. Successful and failed retrieval
trajectories can be distilled into reusable guidance describing evidence
requirements, query patterns, and corrective searches. In long-video
reasoning, this guidance informs subsequent query construction over the
current memory graph, while answer generation remains grounded in
evidence retrieved from the current video ([Fan et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib43)).

After searching, memory selection and prioritization determine which
candidate records receive a higher probability of selection by the
retrieval. In embodied memory, ([Tian et al., 2026](#bib.bib205))
utilizes validated rules to prioritize object records supported by
direct observations, using location, recency, and links to source
evidence to guide retrieval in later tasks. ([Sun et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib196)) updates memory utility estimates from downstream
feedback in clinical settings.

The evolution of memory-management policies benefits from feedback
across the memory lifecycle, as errors introduced at one stage can
affect later stages. Information omitted during writing or lost during
maintenance cannot be recovered through improvements to the retrieval
policy. A failed memory retrieval may therefore reflect earlier
information loss, ineffective retrieval, or incorrect use of retrieved
evidence. Distinguishing the causes of these failures motivates
evaluating writing, maintenance, and retrieval jointly and targeting
policy updates to the mechanisms that contribute to failure.

## 5 Cross-Axis Analysis

|                         |                                    |                                                                                                                         |                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Tier                    | Scope of persistent change         | Core requirement                                                                                                        | Key representational bottlenecks                                                                                                                                                      |
| T1 Static Memory        | None after formation               | Preserve task-relevant information in a form that can be accessed and reused.                                           | Failure to preserve task-relevant information during formation; ineffective access to retained information.                                                                           |
| T2 Dynamic Memory       | Memory state                       | Apply a controlled change to the correct target while preserving unrelated content and dependent representations.       | Limited editability or excessive operation scope; insufficient traces for verifiability; limited reversibility; incomplete update propagation and cross-representation inconsistency. |
| T3 Self-Evolving Memory | Memory state and management policy | Attribute outcomes to policy decisions, revise the responsible policy, and validate the revision across subsequent use. | Limited policy addressability; insufficient policy-decision traceability and feedback attribution; nonpersistent policy revisions; insufficient policy-level validation.              |

Table 1: Representational bottlenecks across memory-management tiers: T1
concerns memory formation and access, T2 adds controlled memory-state
change, and T3 adds policy evaluation and evolution.

Axis I and Axis II describe different aspects of multimodal agent
memory, but they interact in system design. Memory representation
constrains how reliably the operations required at each management tier
can be performed. T1 Static Memory requires fixed memory to be located,
accessed, and reused in downstream reasoning or action. T2 Dynamic
Memory further requires the correct memory units to be updated through a
stable policy, verified, and synchronized across linked representations
without affecting unrelated content. T3 Self-Evolving Memory adds a
stronger requirement: feedback must be attributed to a memory-management
decision, and the relevant writing, maintenance, or retrieval policy
must evolve safely and persistently.

As the scope of persistent change expands from memory state to
management policy, each tier inherits the representational bottlenecks
of the preceding tier and adds another level of uncertainty. As shown in
[Table 1](#S5.T1 "In 5 Cross-Axis Analysis ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory"),
T1 depends on preserving and accessing task-relevant information. T2
additionally depends on correctly changing and coordinating the memory
state. T3 further depends on evaluating these management decisions and
attributing feedback to a reusable policy component.

We therefore examine the representation requirements for T1 Static
Memory, T2 Dynamic Memory, and T3 Self-Evolving Memory, followed by
corpus-level patterns across the two axes.

### 5.1 Representation Requirements for Static Memory

T1 Static Memory imposes the simplest requirement on memory
representation. Once memory has been formed, the system only needs to
find and use it for downstream reasoning or action. The main
representational requirement for T1 Static Memory systems is that memory
formation preserves the information needed for later tasks in a form
that can be effectively accessed and reused. Effective access mechanisms
and retrieval indices must identify the stored context most relevant to
the current query and make it available to the agent ([Yu et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib274); [Fan et al., 2024](#bib.bib44); [Yeo et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib268)). T1 Static Memory requires no persistent memory
change: the fixed memory only needs to be accessed and reused.

### 5.2 Representation Requirements for Dynamic Memory

T2 Dynamic Memory updates memory through a stable management policy. The
memory state changes during use, while the policy that controls these
changes remains stable. Finding and using memory is no longer
sufficient. The system must change the correct memory unit, preserve
unrelated information, and keep dependent representations consistent. We
unfold our discussion into the properties below:

##### Editability

We use editability to describe whether a target memory unit can be
directly modified, replaced, or removed, and at what granularity the
change can be applied. We use operation scope to describe all memory
units, relations, indices, and behaviors affected by the operation,
including both intended and unintended effects. A controlled operation
should have a minimal sufficient scope: it should change the target unit
and its necessary dependencies while preserving unrelated memory.

The available editing scope depends on the representation, which we
categorize them as source-preserving memory and cross-represented
explicit memory. Source-preserving memory allows the system to append,
replace, or remove individual observations. However, a semantic error
may lie in an interpretation derived from the source evidence rather
than in the retained observation itself. If an agent assigns the wrong
identity to a person in a video, the stored frames still record the
visual input available to the agent and need not be modified. The error
lies in the annotation, entity association, or derived record.
Correcting it therefore requires changing the derived representation
rather than the source evidence. Cross-represented explicit memory
exposes facts, events, entities, attributes, and relations as separate
units. These units can be changed directly ([Feng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib46); [Yeo et al., 2026b](#bib.bib269)). However, an
explicit memory unit may have several dependencies. Changing an entity
identity may also require changes to its attributes, event records,
summaries, relations, and retrieval indices. An operation that is too
narrow leaves these dependent records outdated. An operation that is too
broad may change unrelated information. Latent and parametric memory is
harder to edit with a controlled scope. Information may be distributed
across latent states, model weights, or adapters. A state transition or
optimization step can change the representation, but the system may not
know which numerical components encode the target information. The
update may therefore affect unrelated knowledge or behavior.

##### Verifiability

Verifiability asks whether the result of a memory operation can be
checked for correctness. It requires a trace that connects the previous
memory state, the applied operation, the supporting evidence, and the
resulting state. The representation used for verification may differ
from the representation being changed. A revised textual event record
may need to be checked against a video segment, GUI state, audio
interval, or embodied interaction trace. Explicit and source-linked
memory can support this comparison through evidence identifiers and
provenance links. For latent or parametric memory, direct record-level
verification is usually unavailable. The system must instead use
behavioral tests to check whether the intended behavior changed while
unrelated behavior remained stable ([Seong et al., 2025](#bib.bib180)).

##### Reversibility

Reversibility asks whether the memory state preceding that operation can
be restored. Reversal is needed when later evidence, verification, or
downstream outcomes reveal that a memory operation introduced an
incorrect or harmful change, such as overwriting a valid record after an
erroneous entity match. Preserving the original observation alone may
not be sufficient for reversing a memory operation. Regenerating a
summary or structured record from that observation may not reproduce the
previous state when the formation process uses a stochastic model such
as an LLM. Reliable reversal therefore requires a previous version, an
operation log, or an inverse operation. Explicit memory can support
item-level or version-level restoration. Latent and parametric memory
often relies on model checkpoints, which may also remove valid updates
made after the operation being reversed.

##### Update propagation

Update propagation describes how the effects of a memory operation are
carried from one representation to other dependent representations. This
issue arises in hybrid and source-linked memory, where the same
information may be stored in several forms. An operation applied to one
representation may therefore require corresponding changes to the
others. Cross-representation consistency describes whether these
dependent representations remain aligned after the operation.

Propagation must be both complete and selective. Correcting a person’s
identity may require changes to textual records, entity links,
summaries, and retrieval indices, while the original image remains
unchanged as source evidence. A new observation of an object’s location
may update its current-state record and retrieval index while preserving
earlier observations as historical evidence. Under-propagation leaves
outdated or conflicting records. Over-propagation may remove valid
evidence or change unrelated information. Reliable propagation,
therefore, requires links between representations that refer to the same
experience. These links may use timestamps, source identifiers, entity
identifiers, version identifiers, or provenance relations.

The representation requirements for T2 Dynamic Memory are therefore
stronger than those for T1 Static Memory. Source-preserving memory
retains evidence but often lacks direct targets for semantic correction.
Cross-represented explicit memory supports precise edits but requires
provenance, versioning, and dependency tracking. Latent and parametric
memory can be updated, but its update scope is difficult to identify and
verify. Hybrid and source-linked memory supports both explicit
correction and source-based verification, but it must keep its
representations synchronized.

### 5.3 Representation Requirements for Self-Evolving Memory

The representation requirements discussed for T2 Dynamic Memory remain
relevant to T3 Self-Evolving Memory. T3 introduces an additional
meta-level requirement: the system must represent its memory-management
policies, the decisions produced by that policy, and the feedback used
to evaluate and revise it. Self-evolution therefore depends on policy
addressability, policy-level feedback attribution, and persistent,
validated policy revision.

##### Policy Addressability

For a memory-management policy to evolve, the part responsible for a
recurring behavior must provide an identifiable target for revision. It
may be represented explicitly as a rule, instruction, workflow, program,
or retrieval specification, or implicitly in a learned module or
parameter set. Explicit policy representations allow more precise
revisions, whereas distributed representations make the effects of
individual changes harder to isolate.

An explicit memory representation and an explicit policy representation
serve different purposes. The former exposes the content being managed,
whereas the latter exposes the mechanism that determines how this
content is formed, maintained, and accessed. Identifiable memory items
can make a state change easier to inspect, but they do not by themselves
identify which part of the management policy should be revised.

##### Policy Evaluation and Feedback Attribution

T3 must evaluate whether outcomes reveal a recurring weakness in the
memory-management policy rather than an isolated error in the memory
state. This requires connecting an outcome to the memory content
involved, the management decisions that shaped its availability and use,
and the policy component and version that produced those decisions. A
policy-evaluation record may therefore include the relevant task
context, affected memory items, operations performed, retrieved content,
policy version, and subsequent feedback.

This requirement extends the operation-level traceability needed in T2.
In T2, a trace supports verification or reversal of a particular
memory-state change. In T3, traces across interactions support
policy-level attribution: determining whether repeated outcomes justify
changing the reusable mechanism that selects such operations. Feedback
must therefore be sufficiently informative to distinguish failures of
writing, maintenance, retrieval, reasoning, and action. A task-level
reward alone may reveal that the agent failed without identifying which
part of memory management should change.

Axis I constrains what evidence is available for this evaluation.
Explicit memory units, provenance, operation histories, and source links
permit more direct inspection of management decisions. Distributed
latent or parametric representations expose fewer identifiable units and
therefore place greater weight on behavioral evaluation across tasks.
Thus, the memory representation affects how directly the
memory-management design can be evaluated.

##### Persistent and Validated Policy Revision

A policy revision constitutes self-evolution only when it is retained as
part of the reusable memory-management process and affects subsequent
memory operations. The system must therefore represent the revised
policy in a form that can be stored, reapplied, and associated with
later decisions. Maintaining policy versions and their evaluation
histories also supports comparison, auditing, and restoration when a
revision proves harmful.

Validation must assess the revised policy rather than only the
memory-state change that motivated it. Correcting one record
demonstrates that a particular error has been repaired, but it does not
establish that the revised policy will manage future memories more
effectively. Policy-level validation therefore requires subsequent,
replayed, or held-out cases that test both the targeted behavior and
possible regressions in other memory functions.

T3 Self-Evolving Memory requires a meta-level representation that closes
the loop from policy decisions to outcomes, from outcomes to evaluation,
and from evaluation to persistent and validated policy change.
