[Figures 10](#S5.F10 "In 5.4 Corpus-Level Patterns Across the Two Axes ‣ 5 Cross-Axis Analysis ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
and [9](#S5.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ 5.4 Corpus-Level Patterns Across the Two Axes ‣ 5 Cross-Axis Analysis ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
show that multimodal agent memory architectures concentrate in T2
Dynamic Memory across modalities and in the overall corpus, while T3
Self-Evolving Memory remains relatively rare. Of the 297 architectures,
221 (74.4%) update memory state or its management policy during
operation. T2 Dynamic Memory accounts for 204 architectures (68.7% of
the corpus) that update memory through stable management policies,
whereas T3 Self-Evolving Memory accounts for 17 architectures (5.7%)
that update their management policies based on deployment-time feedback.
Stable management policies allow agents to incorporate new experience
through predictable and controllable update procedures, making them the
dominant approach to memory updating.

Hybrid representations help address the competing requirements of
multimodal memory. Hybrid systems constitute 139 of the 297
architectures (46.8%), making them the largest representation category.
Their prevalence suggests that a single representation type is often
insufficient to balance representational fidelity, preservation of
modality-specific detail, retrieval efficiency, and storage cost for
rich multimodal experiences. Hybrid architectures are therefore the most
common representational choice, but they do not dominate the landscape:
many systems address narrower memory problems using the single
representation type best suited to their tasks.

Compact and explicit memory artifacts are the predominant target for
deployment-time policy evolution. Of the 17 T3 Self-Evolving Memory
architectures, 13 are cross-represented systems, while the other 4 are
hybrid systems that include an explicit representation. By contrast, to
the best of our knowledge, neither the source-preserving category nor
the latent or parametric category contains a T3 Self-Evolving Memory
system under our definition. Explicit rules, skills, workflows,
retrieval descriptions, and programs occupy a useful middle ground for
deployment-time evolution: they are more compact and directly editable
than detailed source observations, while remaining more inspectable and
controllable than information distributed across latent states or model
parameters. These properties provide identifiable targets that can be
revised from feedback, validated, and reused in subsequent tasks.

The analysis above characterizes multimodal agent memory at the logical
level: how experience is represented, how memory state and management
policies may change, and what requirements arise from their interaction.
These logical requirements must ultimately be realized by concrete
runtime mechanisms. Memory access requires stored representations to be
located and materialized for computation, while memory updates require
dependent artifacts to remain identifiable, synchronized, and valid as
state changes.
[Section 6](#S6 "6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
therefore examines the systems mechanisms that realize these logical
memory designs under finite compute, memory, storage, and communication
resources.

## 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory

![Refer to caption](2610.19366v1/systems_realization.png)

Figure 11: Systems realization and lifecycle of multimodal agent memory.
A conceptual organization of the mechanisms that connect logical memory
with runtime execution and physical storage, rather than an architecture
implemented in full by any single analyzed system. The control plane
(§[6.4](#S6.SS4 "6.4 Indexing, Reuse, and Scheduling ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory"))
covers logical-memory and execution-state lookup, reuse validation, and
resource-aware admission and scheduling. The cross-layer runtime
(§[6.5](#S6.SS5 "6.5 Materialization and Write-back ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory"))
connects memory to computation through materialization and connects
execution history to retained memory through write-back. The physical
memory hierarchy
(§[6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Physical Storage and Residency ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory"),
§[6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 Data Movement, Compression, and Reconstruction ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory"))
covers residency, replication, transfer, compression, and reconstruction
across accelerator HBM, host DRAM, local SSDs, and remote resources.
Consistency and coordination
(§[6.6](#S6.SS6 "6.6 Consistency and Coordination ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory"))
concern identity, visibility, provenance, invalidation, and isolation
across these paths; the guarantees of individual mechanisms remain
scoped to the artifacts they manage.

### 6.1 Scope and System Abstractions

[Sections 3](#S3 "3 Axis I: Formation and Representation ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory"),
[4](#S4 "4 Axis II: Memory Management ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
and [5](#S5 "5 Cross-Axis Analysis ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
characterize multimodal agent memory at the logical level. Axis I
determines what experience is retained and the operative representation
through which it becomes available to downstream reasoning or action.
Axis II determines whether the system reuses fixed memory, updates
memory state through a stable policy, or evolves the memory-management
policy itself.
[Section 5](#S5 "5 Cross-Axis Analysis ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
further shows that these choices impose requirements on editability,
verifiability, reversibility, and update propagation. This section
examines how those logical representations, operations, and requirements
are realized through physical storage and runtime execution under finite
compute, memory, storage, and communication resources. These
distinctions organize the infrastructure discussion without introducing
an additional axis of the memory taxonomy.

_Logical memory_ denotes the experience-derived state defined in
[Section 2](#S2 "2 Background ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory"),
whose operative representation determines its classification in
[Section 3](#S3 "3 Axis I: Formation and Representation ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory").
When the representation exposes an independently identifiable unit, such
as an image, event record, graph node, or trajectory, we call that unit
a _logical memory object_. This does not assume that every latent state
or parameter update exposes equally addressable semantic units. A
_physical realization_ comprises the concrete records, tensors,
parameter modules, replicas, and auxiliary indices that store this state
or make it accessible. For example, PixelRAG indexes screenshot tiles
using visual embeddings but supplies the retrieved screenshots to the
VLM as source evidence ([Wang et al., 2026j](#bib.bib223)). An index or
storage format therefore supports access to memory without necessarily
defining its operative representation.

_Materialized execution state_ is the runtime form through which
selected memory participates in current computation. Materialization may
assemble textual or visual context, construct model-compatible features
or latent tokens, restore KV states, or activate an experience-specific
parameter module. These are overlapping roles rather than disjoint
storage classes: a retained tensor can be both an operative memory
representation and an artifact used during execution. Mem-W, for
example, constructs latent tokens from retrieved trajectories and
expired in-session history for subsequent agent decisions ([Zhang et
al., 2026b](#bib.bib281)). Conversely, an ordinary request-local
activation or cache does not become agent memory merely because it
occupies storage or accelerates decoding. The relevant criterion is its
deliberate role in retaining experience for later reasoning or action.
Such reuse can occur within a trajectory: TRAM carries auxiliary
recurrent states across reasoning steps while resetting them for each
input ([Liu et al., 2026h](#bib.bib134)). Accordingly, persistence here
concerns the intended reuse horizon; it does not by itself imply
cross-session storage or durability after a process or machine failure.

Logical and physical lifecycles must consequently be distinguished. The
tier migration discussed in
[Section 4.2.4](#S4.SS2.SSS4 "4.2.4 Memory Reorganization ‣ 4.2 T2: Dynamic Memory ‣ 4 Axis II: Memory Management ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
changes a memory’s temporal or functional role, whereas moving an
unchanged artifact from accelerator HBM to host DRAM changes its
residency. Likewise, evicting a reconstructible cache or redundant
replica need not forget the underlying experience. This separation is
conditional on preserving the required information: deleting the last
recoverable copy or applying irreversible lossy transformations can
affect what the agent can subsequently recall. Physical cache
replacement alone does not establish T2 memory-state adaptation, nor
does workload-responsive scheduling alone establish T3 evolution of a
memory-management policy.

Our coverage therefore includes both systems that retain multimodal
experience and transferable mechanisms from model serving, storage, and
retrieval. InferCept’s treatment of tool-interrupted KV state and
SGLang’s prefix reuse provide useful runtime mechanisms, but neither
mechanism alone specifies how an agent forms or revises
experience-derived memory ([Abhyankar et al., 2024](#bib.bib2); [Zheng
et al., 2024](#bib.bib292)). We use such work to explain infrastructure
capabilities and their limits, rather than treating every cache
optimization as a multimodal memory architecture.

Figure
[11](#S6.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
organizes this systems view.
[Sections 6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Physical Storage and Residency ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
and [6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 Data Movement, Compression, and Reconstruction ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
examine where artifacts reside and the cost of moving or reconstructing
them.
[Section 6.4](#S6.SS4 "6.4 Indexing, Reuse, and Scheduling ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
separates evidence relevance, execution-state compatibility, and
scheduling benefit.
[Section 6.5](#S6.SS5 "6.5 Materialization and Write-back ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
considers transformations between retained experience and active
computation, while
[Section 6.6](#S6.SS6 "6.6 Consistency and Coordination ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
examines ownership, visibility, and compatibility across updates. The
remaining integration challenges are discussed in
[Section 8.5](#S8.SS5 "8.5 Memory Infrastructure and Efficiency ‣ 8 Challenges and Outlook ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory").

### 6.2 Physical Storage and Residency

Long-running agents can accumulate substantially more historical state
than an individual request consumes, motivating a separation between
retained memory and its active working set ([Omri et al.,
2026](#bib.bib162)). ReKV provides a multimodal example: it retains
video KV caches beyond the current processing window in RAM or on disk,
then loads the caches of a query-relevant subset of frames for question
answering ([Di et al., 2025](#bib.bib37)). Under a bounded retrieval
budget, retained history can therefore grow without a proportional
increase in the state loaded for each answer. Residency management
determines which artifacts occupy each storage tier, how long physical
copies remain there, and when to promote, demote, replicate, or evict
them.

Storage tiers offer different capacity and access-cost trade-offs.
Accelerator HBM accommodates state used by active inference; host DRAM
can retain inactive state without occupying GPU capacity; and local SSDs
extend retention beyond host memory. ReKV illustrates the latter two
options for historical video KV ([Di et al., 2025](#bib.bib37)).
Placement also extends beyond a single machine. Mooncake pools
cluster-wide DRAM and SSD resources for shared KV retention, while ITME
uses disaggregated, SSD-backed CXL-hybrid memory to expand prefix-cache
capacity ([Qin et al., 2025](#bib.bib169); [Jang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib79)). Network-attached pools and CXL-attached expansion
provide different access paths, not interchangeable latency guarantees.
Moreover, raw media, retrieval embeddings, model-consumed features, and
KV states derived from the same experience need not be co-located: their
sizes, reuse horizons, and reconstruction costs differ.

Tool calls make retention time an explicit decision. InferCept compares
_Preserve_, _Swap_, and _Discard_: keeping intercepted KV on the GPU,
moving it to host memory, or reconstructing it after resumption
([Abhyankar et al., 2024](#bib.bib2)). Continuum adds a time-to-live
(TTL) to GPU retention, balancing the cost of occupying capacity against
avoided reload or recomputation and subsequent queueing delay ([Li et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib107)). TTL expiration ends protection under the
scheduler’s rules; it does not make the remembered evidence semantically
obsolete. MORI instead ranks complete agent programs by recent relative
idleness, retaining busier programs in HBM and more-idle programs in
DRAM ([Xia et al., 2026b](#bib.bib248)). Its sticky placement changes
tiers when capacity pressure requires demotion or available HBM permits
promotion, avoiding migration at every tool-call boundary. These
mechanisms use different signals—interruption cost, retention time, and
program activity—to balance occupancy against resumption overhead.

Distributed reuse introduces a second placement dimension: which nodes
retain an artifact and how many copies are maintained. Mooncake tracks
cache locations and supports replication so that frequently accessed KV
blocks can be available on multiple workers ([Qin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib169)). Local replicas reduce repeated remote access but
increase aggregate storage; shared pools reduce the need to duplicate
every artifact but expose remote-transfer costs. For multimodal memory,
these decisions can be made separately for source media and expensive
derived states. They must also respect the distinction between sharing
an observation and reusing its computation: identical historical
evidence does not imply that its KV state is compatible with every
consuming context.

The central residency trade-off is therefore not simply hot versus cold
storage. It combines expected reuse time, state size, reconstruction
cost, concurrent demand, and access locality. Program admission and
worker selection interact with these decisions, as discussed in
[Section 6.4](#S6.SS4 "6.4 Indexing, Reuse, and Scheduling ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory").
The cost of implementing a residency change depends on the transfer and
restoration mechanisms considered next.

### 6.3 Data Movement, Compression, and Reconstruction

A retained artifact is not necessarily ready for execution. Storage
access, interconnect transfer, decompression, and layout conversion can
delay its use even when lookup succeeds. These costs concern the
restoration path; they are distinct from deciding where an artifact
should reside or whether it is compatible with the current request.

Pipelining reduces the transfer latency exposed on the critical path.
CachedAttention uses layer-wise preloading and asynchronous saving to
overlap KV access with computation ([Gao et al., 2024](#bib.bib47)).
Across nodes, Mooncake supports asynchronous transfers over RDMA-capable
infrastructure and streams newly produced KV toward decode workers
during prefill ([Qin et al., 2025](#bib.bib169)). Buffering enables
overlap but consumes additional memory, and concurrent transfers can
compete with inference for bandwidth. Consequently, an asynchronous
interface alone does not guarantee that restoration is hidden.

Compression and partial recomputation offer complementary ways to reduce
transferred bytes. CacheGen combines quantization and entropy coding
with chunked streaming, overlapping transmission with codec decoding
([Liu et al., 2024a](#bib.bib138)). Cake concurrently recomputes from
the beginning of a reusable prefix and loads cached KV from its end,
adapting the division of work to available computation and I/O resources
([Jin et al., 2025b](#bib.bib90)). The trade-off is therefore among
transferred bytes, codec work, temporary storage, and recomputation.
Lossy compression additionally affects approximation quality. In
particular, a compact transport bitstream need not occupy proportionally
less HBM after it is decoded into inference tensors.

Multimodal and agent workloads provide additional overlap windows. MPIC
loads cached image state while computing missing image caches; this
overlap is distinct from its selective recomputation for contextual
reuse ([Zhao et al., 2025b](#bib.bib291)). TokenCake exploits tool-call
intervals for opportunistic asynchronous offload and predictive upload,
and initiates immediate upload when a tool returns earlier than
predicted ([Bian et al., 2027](#bib.bib13)). Workflow-informed
prefetching also uses anticipated agent execution, as discussed for
KVFlow in
[Section 6.4](#S6.SS4 "6.4 Indexing, Reuse, and Scheduling ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory").
These mechanisms reduce exposed restoration cost when sufficient
independent work is available, but short intervals, prediction errors,
and contention can leave transfers on the critical path. Completing a
transfer establishes availability, not reuse validity.

### 6.4 Indexing, Reuse, and Scheduling

The request-time control path separates three questions: which memory is
relevant, whether a retained execution artifact is compatible, and
whether reusing it is worthwhile. A _logical-memory index_ identifies
accessible evidence or experience; an _execution-state index_ identifies
potentially reusable computation associated with concrete inputs and
execution dependencies. A hit in the first does not imply a hit in the
second, and neither hit alone determines the best execution plan.

Logical-memory access reflects the organization of retained experience.
M3-Agent combines semantic similarity with timestamp-based sequential
retrieval and entity-based associative retrieval over text, image, and
audio memory ([Long et al., 2026](#bib.bib143)). DynaMem couples
language-based localization with a spatial-semantic map and can retrieve
the latest image associated with a selected voxel ([Liu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib135)). These access paths exploit temporal order, entity
links, spatial structure, and modality-bearing evidence. Their results
identify what the agent should inspect; they do not certify the
reusability of tensors previously computed from those objects.

Execution-state indexing instead exploits computational dependencies.
SGLang’s RadixAttention organizes token prefixes and their KV states in
a radix tree, with image hashes representing multimodal inputs within
that indexing scheme ([Zheng et al., 2024](#bib.bib292)). Exact-prefix
reuse requires matching the relevant input prefix and computational
configuration, including positions and model dependencies; an image hash
by itself is insufficient. Prompt Cache enables modular reuse within an
explicitly defined positional schema, whereas CacheBlend selectively
recomputes cached states to restore cross-chunk contextualization ([Gim
et al., 2024](#bib.bib50); [Yao et al., 2025a](#bib.bib266)). MPIC
similarly addresses image-context reuse through position handling and
selective recomputation ([Zhao et al., 2025b](#bib.bib291)). These
methods should not be treated as equivalent guarantees:
schema-constrained reuse and quality-evaluated approximate
reconstruction differ from exact reuse of an unchanged prefix.

Scheduling determines how compatible reuse opportunities interact with
resource demand. SGLang orders requests to exploit common cached
prefixes, while Preble jointly considers prefix reuse and load balancing
when dispatching requests across workers ([Zheng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib292); [Srivatsa et al., 2025](#bib.bib193)). Reusing a
prefix on an overloaded worker can be less attractive than recomputing
it elsewhere. For retrieval-mediated requests, evidence relevance
governs what enters computation, whereas cache locality concerns where
that computation can run efficiently. Neither should silently substitute
for the other.

Agent execution provides signals beyond individual requests.
ThunderAgent treats a complete agent program as a scheduling unit, using
execution phase and context footprint to pause or restore programs under
memory pressure ([Kang et al., 2026](#bib.bib92)). Its global waiting
queue permits paused programs to resume on a worker with available
capacity, rather than requiring their original placement. KVFlow
exploits an exposed Agent Step Graph to estimate steps-to-execution,
prioritize fixed-prefix KV nodes, and prefetch upcoming state from CPU
to GPU ([Pan et al., 2025](#bib.bib165)). Its workflow-level reuse
signal depends on an exposed graph, which may include conditional
branches. Together with MORI’s tier-level admission control ([Xia et
al., 2026b](#bib.bib248)), these designs connect execution readiness to
cache retention and capacity allocation.

Here, admission concerns requests, programs, or physical cache entries,
rather than the semantic decision to write an observation into logical
memory. A useful reuse decision must account for validation, transfer,
reconstruction, queueing, and displaced work, not just the amount of
cached state.
[Section 6.5](#S6.SS5 "6.5 Materialization and Write-back ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
examines the transformations selected by this control path, and
[Section 6.6](#S6.SS6 "6.6 Consistency and Coordination ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
examines how subsequent updates affect their eligibility for reuse.

### 6.5 Materialization and Write-back

Materialization and write-back implement the two directions of the
logical memory lifecycle described in
[Sections 3](#S3 "3 Axis I: Formation and Representation ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
and [4](#S4 "4 Axis II: Memory Management ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory").
On the read path, materialization converts a selected logical memory
representation into model-consumable context, features, latent states,
or parameter modules for current computation. On the write path,
observations, execution history, or completed trajectories are
transformed into persistent state that can subsequently participate in
memory formation or management. The systems concern here is therefore
not what should be remembered or updated, but when these transformations
execute, what artifacts they produce, and what preparation and
consumption costs they impose.

Textual and source-level inputs have different preparation costs.
PixelRAG renders and indexes screenshot tiles during datastore
construction, then supplies retrieved pixels to a VLM. Downsampling
before reading reduces visual-token demand without rebuilding the
datastore or retrieval index ([Wang et al., 2026j](#bib.bib223)). FOLIO
supplies compact semantic records and can recover linked keyframes when
its relevance criterion indicates insufficient grounding ([Fan et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib42)). Reopening images may recover details missing from
an abstraction, but incurs visual encoding and additional model input.
Storage compression, visual-token reduction, and downstream attention
cost are therefore distinct efficiency measures.

Latent-token and KV-based paths move work across different boundaries.
Mem-W uses a visual–textual encoder and a Q-Former-based compressor to
produce a fixed number of soft memory tokens per selected trajectory
segment ([Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib281)). The limit bounds expansion
per segment, not the total cost of encoding or selecting multiple
segments. ReKV instead constructs video KV incrementally before a
question arrives and binds retrieved blocks into question-answering
attention ([Di et al., 2025](#bib.bib37)). Its retrieved tokens receive
consecutive positions rather than their original video positions. This
is part of a specific attention and positional scheme, not evidence that
arbitrary cached tensors can be reused after context changes. Latent
compression pays preparation work to reduce the model-facing input,
whereas KV precomputation moves part of that work ahead of the query and
retains the resulting tensors.

Parametric memory follows a further path that is not captured by context
insertion alone. Frames2LoRA generates a video-specific LoRA adapter
from video-conditioned representations through a trained hypernetwork;
subsequent questions use the adapted model without replaying the
original visual tokens ([Suri et al., 2026](#bib.bib200)). From a
runtime perspective, the relevant artifacts are the generated parameter
module and the backbone to which it is attached. The corresponding costs
include adapter production, retention, loading, and activation, rather
than only context length. This complements the parametric representation
discussion in
[Section 3.3.2](#S3.SS3.SSS2 "3.3.2 Experience-Conditioned Parametric Memory ‣ 3.3 Internalized Latent and Parametric Memory ‣ 3 Axis I: Formation and Representation ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
without treating ordinary pretrained model weights as experience-derived
agent memory.

Write-back must likewise distinguish reuse horizons. Mem-W carries
expired interaction history forward as compressed latent context, while
MementoGUI both compacts older working-memory entries and uses a
separate Episodic Writer to construct source-linked records for later
episodes ([Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib281); [Zeng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib278)). In-session compaction preserves task progress;
episodic write-back creates a cross-episode retrieval artifact. Both can
retain experience for later use, but only episodic write-back crosses
that external episodic-storage boundary. Neither description alone
specifies crash durability. Producing summaries, organizing visual
crops, and constructing retrieval embeddings also consume resources
before later reads can benefit.

Reasoning history can become either recurrent state or procedural
experience. TRAM pools completed-step activations into fast and slow
recurrent states that influence later reasoning within the same input
([Liu et al., 2026h](#bib.bib134)). RRM instead distills completed
retrieval trajectories and feedback into procedural records, excluding
historical answers and video-specific facts; retrieved procedures guide
subsequent evidence acquisition rather than being inserted as factual
answer context ([Fan et al., 2026b](#bib.bib43)). These paths differ in
both what persists and the model interface through which it is reused.

Write-back may produce linked artifacts asynchronously. FOLIO builds
semantic records associated with retained keyframes while a short-term
visual buffer supplies recent evidence; M²A maintains raw message
records alongside editable semantic observations linked by evidence
identifiers ([Fan et al., 2026a](#bib.bib42); [Feng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib46)). Retaining these links enables later source recovery
but entails constructing and maintaining both abstractions and
supporting artifacts. The cost of memory therefore spans construction,
retrieval, and consumption, rather than stored size alone ([Omri et al.,
2026](#bib.bib162)). Publication and update coordination across these
artifacts are considered next.

### 6.6 Consistency and Coordination

Consistency and coordination provide the systems support for the T2
representation requirements identified in
[Section 5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Representation Requirements for Dynamic Memory ‣ 5 Cross-Axis Analysis ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory").
When memory is updated, later reads may encounter different record
versions, physical replicas, or derived execution states. Editability
requires the system to identify the affected logical object and its
physical realizations; verifiability requires provenance and version
information connecting the update to supporting evidence; reversibility
requires an earlier version, operation log, checkpoint, or
reconstructible source; and update propagation requires dependent
artifacts to be refreshed or invalidated. Coordination determines when
these changes become visible and which versions or derivatives remain
eligible for use. Deciding whether new evidence should revise a belief
remains a memory-management question, whereas publishing the selected
revision consistently across access paths is a systems question.

Update ownership and evidence identity provide a starting point. M²A
gives its MemoryManager exclusive read–write access to the memory bank
and links semantic observations to supporting messages ([Feng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib46)). This identifies an application-level owner and
evidence trail, not a distributed transaction protocol. When a
dependency changes, the associated derivation must be refreshed or its
compatibility re-established before it is used for a request requiring
the revised state. Historical queries may still use an earlier version
when its temporal scope and access permissions permit. This selective
treatment avoids invalidating unchanged source evidence merely because
an interpretation has been corrected.

Publication rules determine what readers see while writes proceed. FOLIO
excludes segment records still being written and instead answers from
completed memory and recent visual context ([Fan et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib42)). Manu coordinates vector-store subscribers through
timestamped logs and time-tick progress markers, allowing queries to
wait for a configured freshness level ([Guo et al., 2022](#bib.bib59)).
These mechanisms operate at different boundaries: application records in
the former and indexed data with row-level ACID support in the latter.
Their guarantees do not automatically compose into atomic publication
across separately maintained media, semantic records, retrieval indices,
and model-side states.

Shared execution state also requires lifetime and aliasing control.
Mooncake tracks prefix-dependent cache blocks and their replicas and
protects blocks used by ongoing requests from eviction ([Qin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib169)). Within an inference engine, vLLM uses
reference-counted block sharing and copy-on-write when a sequence
extends a shared KV block ([Kwon et al., 2023](#bib.bib96)). These
mechanisms prevent premature reclamation and interference between
branches, but do not determine whether the underlying memory has become
stale. Similarly, Manu’s deletion bitmaps suppress deleted vectors in
search before segment-index rebuilding ([Guo et al., 2022](#bib.bib59)).
Read exclusion, storage reclamation, and invalidation of derived
representations are separate operations.

Authorization imposes another visibility boundary. Collaborative Memory
separates private and shared fragments and uses provenance and a current
access graph to filter retrieval as permissions change ([Rezazadeh et
al., 2025](#bib.bib177)). This controls exposure through its retrieval
interface; it does not demonstrate retroactive removal of information
already materialized in another agent’s context or KV state.
Authorization is consequently distinct from copy-on-write: one governs
who may consume an artifact, while the other protects shared physical
state against a branch’s mutations.

Compatibility can change even when source observations do not. FastFill
aligns embeddings across model updates and prioritizes partial
backfilling using alignment uncertainty ([Jaeckle et al.,
2023](#bib.bib77)). This addresses retrieval features, not arbitrary
model-consumed latent memory. DroidSpeak selectively recomputes layer
groups when reusing KV across profiled fine-tuned model variants ([Liu
et al., 2026k](#bib.bib139)); its scope is model-pair-specific, and
substantial distribution drift can degrade quality. Compatibility
therefore depends on the producer, consumer, and validated
transformation, not source identity alone.

The analyzed mechanisms coordinate particular records, retrieval views,
or execution blocks. Their combination exposes trade-offs among
freshness, read latency, sharing, bookkeeping, and reconstruction. A
retained historical observation can remain valid after a current-state
record changes, while an unchanged physical cache can become
incompatible with a new consumer. Establishing explicit guarantees
across these boundaries is the integration problem developed in
[Section 8.5](#S8.SS5 "8.5 Memory Infrastructure and Efficiency ‣ 8 Challenges and Outlook ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory").
[Sections 6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Physical Storage and Residency ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
and [6.6](#S6.SS6 "6.6 Consistency and Coordination ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
do not introduce new memory types; they characterize the runtime
conditions under which the representation and management choices in
[Sections 3](#S3 "3 Axis I: Formation and Representation ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory"),
[4](#S4 "4 Axis II: Memory Management ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
and [5](#S5 "5 Cross-Axis Analysis ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
can be served efficiently, consistently, and within finite resources.

## 7 Evaluation and Applications

[Section 5](#S5 "5 Cross-Axis Analysis ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
analyzes how representation constrains memory management, while
[Section 6](#S6 "6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
examines how the resulting designs are realized at runtime. This section
characterizes how multimodal memory systems are evaluated and what
functions memory serves in their applications.
[Section 7.1](#S7.SS1 "7.1 Evaluation Dimensions for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ 7 Evaluation and Applications ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
defines the capabilities that memory benchmarks attempt to measure,
[Section 7.2](#S7.SS2 "7.2 Benchmark Landscape Across Modalities ‣ 7 Evaluation and Applications ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
characterizes the 82 benchmark records by evaluation setting,
[Section 7.3](#S7.SS3 "7.3 Application Regimes ‣ 7 Evaluation and Applications ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
describes the functions memory serves in deployed systems, and
[Section 7.4](#S7.SS4 "7.4 Application–Evaluation Alignment and Gaps ‣ 7 Evaluation and Applications ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
reports what those benchmarks do and do not exercise. What the field
should do about the gaps recorded here is argued in
[Section 8](#S8 "8 Challenges and Outlook ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory").

### 7.1 Evaluation Dimensions for Multimodal Agent Memory

End-task accuracy alone cannot establish whether an agent has used
memory: a correct output may follow from the current context or
parametric knowledge, while an error may arise during memory formation,
access, maintenance, or utilization. Recent benchmarks therefore
increasingly evaluate not only task outcomes, but also the evidence and
state transitions supporting them ([Ren et al., 2026](#bib.bib176); [Liu
et al., 2026c](#bib.bib128)). Accordingly,
[Table 2](#S7.T2 "In 7.2 Benchmark Landscape Across Modalities ‣ 7 Evaluation and Applications ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
characterizes each benchmark through shared memory capabilities,
modality-specific requirements, and evaluation settings. The six shared
dimensions capture three stages of memory use.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

These dimensions are modality-independent: they characterize whether
memory preserves sufficient evidence, remains valid under change, and
contributes to downstream decisions.

Shared dimensions alone, however, cannot express the internal structure
that must survive within each modality. Image-memory benchmarks
therefore distinguish fine-grained visual-detail retention (FG), entity
tracking across observations (ET), and visual state-change tracking
(VC). Video benchmarks add temporal localization (TL), temporal-relation
reasoning over event order and duration (TR), and multi-event evidence
integration (ME) ([Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib282); [Wang et al.,
2026i](#bib.bib222)). Audio and speech benchmarks require speaker
tracking (SP), acoustic-cue retention (AC), and repair persistence (RP).
SP tests whether a memory preserves who spoke across turns or sessions;
AC tests whether it retains non-lexical evidence such as prosody, vocal
style, and background sound; and RP tests whether spoken feedback or
later evidence produces a persistent correction rather than a transient
response ([Xie et al., 2026c](#bib.bib254); [Jiang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib86); [Chattopadhyay et al., 2026](#bib.bib19)). GUI
evaluation emphasizes persistent interface state (GS), associations
between actions and resulting states (AO), and reuse of experience
across sessions (XR) ([Liu et al., 2026d](#bib.bib129)). Embodied
benchmarks instead require spatial memory (SM), object-state tracking
under partial observability (OS), and task-state or progress tracking
(TS) ([Hu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib69); [Yadav et al.,
2026](#bib.bib259)). These dimensions expose representational failures
that long-range or cross-modal labels cannot: an agent may retain an
event while losing its precise time, remember an object while failing to
preserve its location, or recall a GUI action without the state
transition it produced.

The capability annotations should be interpreted together with the
benchmark setup recorded in
[Table 2](#S7.T2 "In 7.2 Benchmark Landscape Across Modalities ‣ 7 Evaluation and Applications ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory").
The data source distinguishes real, synthetic, simulated, and hybrid
settings, which differ in perceptual complexity, environmental control,
and the availability of counterfactual conditions. The task field
identifies whether memory supports question answering, retrieval,
localization, generation, action, planning, learning, or mapping. The
ground-truth field records what can be verified, including answers,
supporting evidence, regions, timestamps, environment states, actions,
provenance, and reliability labels. Answer-only supervision evaluates
end-task correctness but provides limited evidence that the intended
memory was used. By contrast, evidence, region, timestamp, and
provenance annotations support more direct evaluation of memory
grounding, while state and action supervision connect memory to
interactive behavior. These setup dimensions therefore determine how
precisely a benchmark can attribute success or failure to memory, even
when two benchmarks nominally cover the same capability.

These dimensions also connect benchmark coverage to the taxonomy
introduced earlier. CE and the modality-specific dimensions primarily
specify the evidence, attributes, and relations that memory formation
must preserve and make accessible, and therefore connect most directly
to Axis I. LE, TL, ME, and XR probe the storage, access, and reuse of
fixed memory and therefore align with T1 Static Memory, whereas SC, CF,
VC, GS, AO, OS, and TS can expose demands for state maintenance or
revision under changing observations and therefore inform evaluation of
T2 Dynamic Memory. Offline reconstruction of a state history, however,
does not by itself establish deployment-time memory updating. UQ and MA
primarily evaluate memory utilization through evidence sufficiency and
action selection. None of these labels alone establishes T3
Self-Evolving Memory, which requires deployment feedback to produce
persistent changes to a reusable memory-management policy. This mapping
supports the lifecycle-based coverage analysis in
[Section 7.4](#S7.SS4 "7.4 Application–Evaluation Alignment and Gaps ‣ 7 Evaluation and Applications ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory").

### 7.2 Benchmark Landscape Across Modalities

[Table 2](#S7.T2 "In 7.2 Benchmark Landscape Across Modalities ‣ 7 Evaluation and Applications ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
organizes 82 selected benchmark resources and evaluation protocols by
their evaluation setting. The selection includes dedicated memory tests
and broader tasks used to evaluate systems that retain and reuse
multimodal experience. Such tasks can reveal the contribution of memory
even when their scores also depend on perception, reasoning, planning,
or execution. Selected text-only and semantic-state protocols provide
comparisons for shared memory functions; they do not establish visual or
acoustic retention. Inclusion therefore indicates evaluation relevance,
while the capability annotations describe what each protocol directly or
indirectly measures. Beyond differences in sensory input, these groups
vary in the experience that must persist, the horizon over which it is
reused, and the supervision available to verify its contribution.

|   Table notes Legend. ✓ = directly evaluated; $`\circ`$ = partial or indirect coverage; ✗ = not evaluated. A check indicates that the benchmark contains a scored task for which the corresponding memory demand is necessary to produce the correct answer or action. #### 7.2.1 Image Memory

Image benchmarks typically treat memory as a collection of visual
episodes associated with dialogue, time, location, or personal context.
Their horizons range from multi-turn image sequences to persistent
personal archives, with question answering and retrieval as the dominant
tasks. These resources differ in whether evaluation uses images directly
or substitutes textual descriptions, as well as in the stages of the
memory lifecycle they exercise.

LoCoMo ([Maharana et al., 2024](#bib.bib149)) evaluates long-term
conversational memory through question answering, event summarization,
and multimodal dialogue generation. Its conversations include shared
images, but the original QA and summarization experiments replace images
with captions; images are used directly only in dialogue generation.

Evidence-centered benchmarks provide the clearest tests of visual
persistence. Memory-QA ([Jiang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib84)) evaluates
recall over real-world multimodal records, requiring temporal or
location cues and evidence distributed across multiple memories.
DISBench ([Deng et al., 2026](#bib.bib36)) instead evaluates
context-aware retrieval and localization within interconnected visual
histories, while MemLens ([Ren et al., 2026](#bib.bib176)) stresses
whether fine-grained visual evidence survives long-term storage and
retrieval.

Personalized and conversational benchmarks extend evaluation from
evidence access to memory validity. LCMP ([Hong et al.,
2026](#bib.bib67)) and ATM-Bench ([Mei et al., 2026](#bib.bib151))
distribute user-specific attributes and references across multiple
sources and sessions, requiring the agent to track both persistent and
changing information. MemEye ([Guo et al., 2026b](#bib.bib56)) evaluates
image-grounded histories and visual state changes, while Mem-Gallery
([Bei et al., 2026](#bib.bib12)) and H2HMem ([Zhu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib295)) additionally test conflicting records and
insufficient evidence. These benchmarks test whether retrieved memories
remain current and mutually consistent, although updates are usually
defined by curated histories rather than by an evolving
memory-management policy. MemLeak ([Wang and Zhang, 2026](#bib.bib214))
examines a complementary requirement: whether facts requested for
deletion remain recoverable from retained text or images.

A group connects image memory to action or source verification. SMMBench
([Chai et al., 2026](#bib.bib17)) distributes evidence across
conversations, screenshots, images, tables, and documents, and provides
answer, evidence, and provenance supervision for memory-grounded
decisions. EMemBench ([Li et al., 2026k](#bib.bib115)) similarly
introduces state or action consequences, but such supervision remains
uncommon. Conversational benchmarks span broader dialogue evaluation and
explicit memory tasks: MMDU ([Liu et al., 2024b](#bib.bib142)) evaluates
multi-image, multi-turn response quality, whereas MMRC ([Xue et al.,
2025](#bib.bib258)) includes memory recall, image management, and
information updates. Their aggregate scores nevertheless combine memory
with other dialogue capabilities. Across these settings, supervision
remains predominantly answer- and evidence-based, while provenance,
state, reliability, and action labels appear only in a smaller subset.
Current image evaluation therefore covers fine-grained evidence
retention, entity continuity, and visual state change more thoroughly
than extended interaction or adaptive memory use. Provenance and
behavioral verification also remain comparatively underdeveloped.

#### 7.2.2 Video Memory

Video-memory evaluation has expanded from offline retrieval over
completed recordings to causally constrained streaming and interactive
assistance, but it remains dominated by readout-style question
answering. We group current benchmarks into three evaluation regimes:
fixed-recording or lifelog recall, causal streaming evaluation, and
future-oriented interactive assistance. Although all three require
access to past video, they differ in whether evidence is available as a
completed record, arrives incrementally, or must influence subsequent
interaction.

Fixed-recording and lifelog benchmarks provide the clearest tests of
long-range temporal access. M3-Bench ([Long et al., 2026](#bib.bib143))
and HippoVlog ([Lin et al., 2026d](#bib.bib124)) cover extended
audiovisual streams, while EgoLifeQA ([Yang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib263))
uses week-long multimodal egocentric records to support event recall,
personalized question answering, and recommendation. EgoMonth ([Chen et
al., 2026f](#bib.bib25)) extends the horizon to month-scale experience,
and EgoMem ([Zuo et al., 2025](#bib.bib299)) emphasizes backtracking
through long videos. EgoMemReason ([Wang et al., 2026l](#bib.bib229))
further separates entity, event, and behavioral memory. LVOmniBench
([Tao et al., 2026](#bib.bib204)) broadens this setting beyond
egocentric data by requiring joint reasoning over long-form audio and
video. These benchmarks are strong tests of temporal localization and
long-range evidence retrieval, with answers established primarily
through timestamps or supporting evidence, but they usually assume that
the relevant video history is already available as a completed record.

Streaming evaluation introduces causal evidence availability. VStream-QA
([Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib282)) and StreamingBench ([Lin et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib122)) ask questions while the video continues to arrive,
whereas StreamBench ([Xiong et al., 2025](#bib.bib255)) adds multi-round
interaction over hierarchically maintained short- and long-term records.
Causal access makes these benchmarks closer to deployment, but does not
by itself establish that a model maintains or revises a persistent
memory state. Multi-view benchmarks add a distinct challenge: memory
must align temporally related evidence across agents, cameras, or
viewpoints rather than retrieve from a single chronological stream.
MA-EgoQA ([Kim et al., 2026](#bib.bib94)) constructs a shared history
from synchronized egocentric streams and requires the model to identify
and combine agent-specific evidence, while EgoExoMem ([Liu et al.,
2026i](#bib.bib136)) introduces cross-view temporal and spatial
dependencies. These settings therefore test distributed perspective and
evidence fusion, not merely access to a longer video, although they
still treat memory chiefly as a retained record to be queried rather
than as a state that must be actively maintained.

A smaller group evaluates whether video memory supports future behavior.
VideoWebArena ([Jang et al., 2025](#bib.bib80)) tests factual and skill
retention from tutorials during subsequent web tasks, scoring
intermediate answers and final environment states. Because video-derived
information can remain in context, these scores do not isolate
memory-management quality. RIVER Bench ([Shi et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib185)) and StreamArena ([Zhang et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib286)) combine historical recall with live or proactive
responses under real-time constraints, while StreamMemBench ([Liu et
al., 2026e](#bib.bib130)) tests whether observed evidence, feedback, and
prior interaction are reused in a later task. SLVMBench ([Yang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib264)) further asks agents to extract procedural knowledge
from recorded experience and apply it to a live stream. These tasks move
beyond retrospective recall toward stateful assistance, but still mainly
test whether prior experience is reused, not whether deployment feedback
changes the memory-management policy itself.

Across these settings, supervision remains predominantly answer-,
evidence-, and timestamp-based. Overall, video benchmarks evaluate
temporal localization, long-range event relations, and multi-event
integration more thoroughly than most other modalities. However,
conflict resolution, unanswerable queries, and memory-grounded action
remain less common in
[Figure 12](#S7.F12 "In 7.2.2 Video Memory ‣ 7.2 Benchmark Landscape Across Modalities ‣ 7 Evaluation and Applications ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory");
source-level provenance and feedback-driven policy change are also
weakly evaluated. This gap contrasts with the architectural trend in
[Figure 8](#S5.F8 "In 5.4 Corpus-Level Patterns Across the Two Axes ‣ 5 Cross-Axis Analysis ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory"):
memory systems commonly update state, yet video benchmarks rarely verify
whether deployment feedback produces persistent improvements in the
memory-management policy.
