#### 7.2.3 Audio and Speech Memory

Audio and speech occupy a small but differentiated part of the benchmark
landscape. Existing evaluations span persistent voice-grounded
conversational memory, memory over streaming audiovisual experience,
retrieval from a fixed long-form recording, and short-horizon speech
state carried or revised across turns. These audio-based settings
exercise different parts of the memory lifecycle; text-only preference
protocols provide a separate comparison.

ChatMem-Bench, introduced with VoiceMem ([Xie et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib254)), evaluates long-horizon speech memory using 316
questions over 53 hours of dialogue. Human-curated synthetic histories
support tasks covering information updates, abstention, persona,
affective attribution, speaker association, and non-lexical acoustic
evidence. Its published category scores support direct SC, UQ, SP, and
AC coverage, but only indirect CF and RP coverage: the construction
pipeline includes contradictions, while a dedicated persistent
spoken-repair protocol is not specified. The paper defers detailed
annotation methodology to a follow-up report. EgoMem ([Yao et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib267)) instead combines face and voice identity with
asynchronously managed facts, preferences, and social relations for
later personalized dialogue.

Streaming audiovisual benchmarks broaden the horizon but make audio
attribution less clean. M3-Bench, TeleEgo, and Video-SALMONN S retain or
evaluate audiovisual experience over long streams, yet their
video-centred tasks rarely isolate speaker, prosodic, or non-speech
acoustic retention ([Long et al., 2026](#bib.bib143); [Yan et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib260); [Sun et al., 2026a](#bib.bib195)). Fixed-recording
benchmarks provide more controlled audio evidence: PlanRAG-Audio and
LongAudioQA evaluate planned retrieval from long recordings, while
ChronosAudio and AudioMarathon stress length generalization and temporal
reasoning ([Someki et al., 2026](#bib.bib189); [Tang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib201); [Luo et al., 2026b](#bib.bib146); [He et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib62); [Gong et al., 2025](#bib.bib51)). Because their
memory remains fixed after formation, these settings primarily evaluate
access and reuse in T1 Static Memory rather than cross-session memory
updating.

Interactive ASR supplies a narrower form of state change. Agentic ASR
evaluates whether spoken feedback repairs a transcription state, whereas
Beyond Fresh Starts carries or rolls back acoustic and linguistic state
across utterance boundaries ([Jiang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib86);
[Chattopadhyay et al., 2026](#bib.bib19)). CarMem ([Kirmayr et al.,
2025](#bib.bib95)) provides a text-only comparison for preference
extraction, retrieval, and maintenance. Its voice-assistant application
does not make these experiments tests of acoustic memory. Current
benchmarks therefore cover acoustic retention, long-range retrieval,
speaker association, and repair separately, but rarely combine
cross-session acoustic memory, conflicting spoken evidence, explicit
revision, and memory-grounded action.

#### 7.2.4 GUI Memory

GUI benchmarks occupy a compact but functionally differentiated part of
the evaluation landscape. Existing settings span cross-step state
retention, cross-session experience reuse, personalized and proactive
interaction, and controlled diagnosis of visual memory. All reuse prior
interface experience, but differ in whether memory must preserve a
transient state, recover an action outcome, transfer a workflow, or
retain visual evidence unavailable from text alone.

MemGUI-Bench ([Liu et al., 2026d](#bib.bib129)) provides the broadest
direct evaluation of mobile-agent memory. Its tasks span multiple
applications and use mirrored interactions to separate within-session
retention from cross-session improvement, while hierarchical evaluation
measures memory fidelity, learning effectiveness, and execution
efficiency. MementoGUI-Bench ([Zeng et al., 2026](#bib.bib278)) instead
formulates long-horizon GUI execution as a memory-control problem:
working memory preserves task-relevant interface events and localized
visual evidence, whereas episodic memory retrieves reusable
trajectories. Together, these benchmarks evaluate GUI-state tracking,
action–outcome associations, and experience reuse through regions, task
progress, and action supervision.

Personalized and controlled settings test complementary aspects of state
maintenance. KnowU-Bench ([Chen et al., 2026e](#bib.bib24)) hides the
user profile and requires agents to infer preferences from behavioral
histories, request missing information, and calibrate proactive
intervention in an interactive mobile environment. Its task scores
evaluate the use of history in personalized assistance, while also
depending on preference inference, interaction, and execution.
Memory-World ([Wang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib213)), introduced with STAMP,
programmatically controls what transient interface information must be
stored and later reused, enabling state- and action-verified evaluation
in a simulated environment. DataScope ([Liu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib127))
combines synthetic task data with real mobile applications in 96
cross-page and cross-application workflows. Terminal success, app-level
progress, and Scope-F1 verify which required operations were completed
and which distractors were modified from the resulting application
states; they do not provide expert action-sequence ground truth or
evaluate cross-session reuse. Such benchmarks improve experimental
control, although their synthetic states do not fully reproduce the
variability of real applications.

DMV-Bench ([Tang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib203)) isolates visual memory
more directly by injecting pixel-specific incidental cues into products
visited across autonomous shopping sessions. Textual descriptions cannot
recover the relevant cue, and successful navigation therefore depends on
retaining and retrieving visual evidence with its source provenance.
Current GUI evaluation consequently provides strong coverage of
long-range state tracking, action outcomes, and memory-grounded
execution. It remains weaker on conflicting histories, unanswerable or
unsafe requests, robustness to interface change, and persistent
evolution of memory-management policies. Moreover, endpoint task success
alone may still fail to identify whether an error arose during memory
formation, retrieval, or action selection.

#### 7.2.5 Embodied Memory

Embodied-memory benchmarks assess whether agents can retain and use
experience while navigating, mapping, and manipulating partially
observable environments. Because an agent’s actions affect both the
environment and the observations available later, memory must preserve
spatial structure, maintain object and task states, and associate
actions with their consequences. Existing benchmarks can be organized
into three complementary regimes: navigation and mapping,
memory-dependent manipulation, and long-horizon stateful interaction.

Navigation and mapping benchmarks primarily assess spatial persistence.
FindingDory ([Yadav et al., 2026](#bib.bib259)) requires agents to
retrieve prior visual experience for subsequent navigation and action in
tasks that can be procedurally extended to longer horizons, whereas
3DMem-Bench ([Hu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib69)) evaluates long-term
spatiotemporal question answering, scene captioning, and task execution
in dynamic multi-room environments. SpaMEM ([Liao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib120)) isolates action-conditioned revision of spatial
beliefs, while HIOcc ([Zhu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib294)) evaluates local
occupancy prediction and causal room- and building-level mapping. HIOcc
measures map accuracy, online stability, and revisit consistency in
static scenes; these support direct spatial-memory coverage but only
partial state-change and object-state coverage, without task-progress or
downstream-action evaluation. FindingDory, 3DMem-Bench, and SpaMEM
additionally assess object histories or updates. Spatial regions, maps,
and environment states provide supervision beyond terminal task success.

Other embodied settings assess experience reuse through planning or
active perception. MEMORA-Bench ([Yu et al., 2026d](#bib.bib277)) pairs
recall over participant-specific egocentric histories with generated
plans for observed and novel goals. Its explicit
information-not-available controls directly evaluate UQ, while
plan-order, object-coverage, and preference scores evaluate prospective
memory use; spatial, object-state, and task-progress tracking are only
indirectly covered by these aggregate tasks. APRS ([Tang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib202)) evaluates sequential viewpoint selection and target
segmentation within static panoramas, scoring search success,
efficiency, and mask quality. Expert action trajectories support
training rather than serving as benchmark action ground truth. SIS-Bench
([Zou et al., 2026b](#bib.bib298)) combines landmark and action recall
with spatial reasoning and multiple-choice path planning over UAV
videos. Its planning answers provide indirect MA coverage, not evidence
of executed control or online task-progress tracking.

Manipulation benchmarks assess whether policies preserve action-relevant
history. LIBERO-Mem ([Chung et al., 2026](#bib.bib32)) introduces
non-Markovian tasks that require object histories beyond the current
observation, with object masks, instance identities, and subgoal
annotations. MIKASA-Robo ([Cherepanov et al., 2026](#bib.bib29)),
evaluated here in its simulated RGB+joints setting, tests delayed object
recall, spatial tracking, and sequential action. RMBench ([Chen et al.,
2026d](#bib.bib23)) and ReMemBench ([Shah et al., 2026](#bib.bib181))
provide controlled memory-dependent manipulation tasks. RoboMME ([Dai et
al., 2026](#bib.bib34)) evaluates temporal, spatial, object, and
procedural memory in vision–language–action policies, while RoboMemArena
([Lei et al., 2026](#bib.bib101)) extends evaluation to longer tasks
with subtask and keyframe annotations and paired real-world tasks.
State- and action-level supervision provides direct evidence for
memory-grounded action (MA), although endpoint success cannot
distinguish memory failures from errors in perception, planning, or
control.

Long-horizon and cross-session benchmarks evaluate whether memory
remains valid as world state and interaction history evolve. WorldLines
([Zhang et al., 2026d](#bib.bib287)) pairs evidence-linked memory
questions with embodied planning over semantic household traces; this
protocol evaluates state maintenance without establishing raw visual or
acoustic retention. WorldMemArena ([Liu et al., 2026c](#bib.bib128))
evaluates memory formation, maintenance, retrieval, and use across
multi-session action–world interaction. RoboMME-Interference ([Rathi,
2026](#bib.bib174)) measures retrieval robustness as unrelated prior
sessions accumulate. WorldLines and WorldMemArena therefore extend
evaluation from access to T1 Static Memory toward maintenance and
revision under T2 Dynamic Memory, whereas RoboMME-Interference isolates
interference during access. Most current benchmarks nevertheless rely on
simulated or hybrid environments, and few systematically test
conflicting memories (CF), unanswerable queries (UQ), lifelong updating
in physical environments, or failure attribution across memory-lifecycle
stages.

### 7.3 Application Regimes

Application regimes are distinguished here by the function memory serves
rather than by input modality. They consolidate concrete downstream
tasks—including multimodal recall, long-form video and audio
understanding, personalized interaction, GUI automation, embodied
control, and iterative generation—according to the role memory plays in
the resulting system. This view is orthogonal to Axis I: the same
images, audio, documents, or interaction traces may be retained to
support evidence-based decisions, continuity with a user, execution in
an environment, or consistency in generated content. Each regime
consequently stresses a different property of memory.

#### 7.3.1 Recall and Evidence-Based Reasoning

This regime encompasses multimodal question answering, episodic
retrieval, and long-form video or audio understanding. Although these
tasks operate over different evidence—from visual details and temporally
distributed events to speakers and acoustic cues—they share the
requirement that later outputs remain grounded in recoverable
observations ([Jiang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib84); [Yang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib263); [Someki et al., 2026](#bib.bib189)). Personal
archives and long-document assistants require cross-modal retrieval and
source grounding, whereas enterprise analysis additionally requires
evidence to remain attributable across files, reporting periods, and
tool outputs. MARDoc, for example, distils long-document interaction
traces into structured evidence and reasoning memories and checks
whether the recovered evidence is sufficient ([Chen et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib21)). Financial reasoning makes the temporal and
numerical demands especially explicit: FinAcumen selectively reuses
successful strategies and failure-derived cautions while coordinating
retrieval, visual decoding, calculation, and verification over text,
tables, charts, and time-indexed records ([Guo et al.,
2026d](#bib.bib58)). The central memory property is therefore not recall
volume alone, but recoverable provenance and temporal validity, since
persistence without these safeguards can retain stale or weakly grounded
evidence.

#### 7.3.2 Personalization and Cross-Session Continuity

Personalization uses memory to maintain a user-specific state across
otherwise disconnected encounters. Relevant experience may include
stated preferences, prior dialogue, viewed media, corrections, and
recurring activity patterns. M²A combines complementary memory layers
for long-term multimodal interaction, TAME maintains a state-aware
personalized context without additional training, and Persode grounds a
visual-journaling assistant in episodic personal history ([Feng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib46); [Hong et al., 2026](#bib.bib67); [Jin et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib88)). In consumer settings, the resulting continuity
supports recommendations and assistance; analogous requirements arise in
enterprise workflows that carry user, team, or account context across
sessions. More recently, LLM-based individual simulation has attracted
growing interest. The pioneering Individual Turing Test highlights the
value of memory in capturing personal opinions and preferences ([Guo et
al., 2026c](#bib.bib57)), which could be more faithful through
multimodal personal histories beyond text. This regime stresses identity
scoping, selective retention, and revision: useful continuity requires
the agent to associate evidence with the correct subject and to update
preferences without allowing obsolete or cross-user information to
persist.

#### 7.3.3 Control and Task Execution

Control applications require memory to change what an agent does, not
merely what it can report. They include GUI workflow automation, spatial
navigation and mapping, embodied manipulation and planning, and the
transfer of procedures learned from demonstrations or prior experience
([Wen et al., 2022](#bib.bib233); [Lee et al., 2025](#bib.bib100);
[Liang et al., 2022](#bib.bib119); [Mandlekar et al.,
2023](#bib.bib150); [Garrett et al., 2025](#bib.bib49); [Hsu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib68); [Li et al., 2026f](#bib.bib110)). MAGNET, for
instance, evolves visual-semantic and procedural memories so that GUI
skills transfer across changing interfaces ([Sun et al.,
2026d](#bib.bib198)). In embodied settings, remembered layouts, object
states, and task progress support navigation and manipulation under
partial observability, while environment states and action outcomes
provide direct evidence of memory utility ([Yadav et al.,
2026](#bib.bib259); [Dai et al., 2026](#bib.bib34); [Liu et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib128); [Bjorck et al., 2026](#bib.bib14); [Ma et al.,
2025](#bib.bib147)). The same principle extends to other domains.
FinAgent combines numerical, textual, and visual market evidence with
diversified memory retrieval and dual-level reflection to adapt its
decisions as market conditions change ([Zhang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib284)). Enterprise automation adds operational constraints
and heterogeneous artifacts: Matrix refines experience-derived memory to
specialize agents for recurring business-document extraction, while
MemoPhishAgent retrieves episodic reasoning trajectories to orchestrate
tools for recurring and novel phishing threats ([Liu et al.,
2026f](#bib.bib131); [Chen et al., 2026g](#bib.bib26)). The defining
property is action relevance under change: stored experience must
improve the present decision while remaining revisable when interfaces,
environments, document formats, market conditions, or threat patterns
evolve.

#### 7.3.4 Generation and World Consistency

Generative applications use memory to preserve constraints, entities,
style, and causal state across iterative production. Unlike recall and
control, however, this regime remains weakly represented by dedicated
memory benchmarks: existing generation tasks commonly evaluate
open-ended responses rather than image, video, or speech synthesis with
persistent identity and world state. Application systems nevertheless
demonstrate the underlying demand. MemSlides separates profile, working,
and tool memories to support personalized slide creation and local
revision, while agentic video systems retain executable event structures
to keep generated scenes aligned with an evolving plan ([Jin et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib91); [Cudlenco et al., 2026](#bib.bib33)). Financial
reporting combines this consistency requirement with evidence grounding.
FinSight’s variable memory unifies financial data, tools, and
intermediate analyses before synthesizing citation-aware narratives,
tables, and charts ([Jin et al., 2026a](#bib.bib87)). Here memory is
valuable because generation is not a single decoding pass: evidence is
collected, transformed, assessed, visualized, and revised over multiple
stages. The regime therefore stresses versioned state and recoverable
dependencies, so that a change to an underlying fact or analytical
result can propagate coherently through the final multimodal artifact.

### 7.4 Application–Evaluation Alignment and Gaps

The benchmark landscape is broader in modality than in lifecycle
coverage. This pattern is partly determined by the downstream tasks used
for evaluation. Image, video, and audio benchmarks predominantly use
question answering, retrieval, or localization, which expose recall and
grounding but provide limited evidence of subsequent memory use. GUI and
embodied benchmarks instead evaluate action or planning through
interface states, environment transitions, and task success ([Liu et
al., 2026d](#bib.bib129); [Yadav et al., 2026](#bib.bib259); [Liu et
al., 2026c](#bib.bib128)). The task therefore determines which aspects
of memory can be observed, whereas the capability dimensions
characterize the memory demands being evaluated.

This task dependence leads to uneven coverage across the application
regimes in
[Section 7.3](#S7.SS3 "7.3 Application Regimes ‣ 7 Evaluation and Applications ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory").
Long-range and cross-modal evidence access supports many important
applications and, correspondingly, constitutes the dominant evaluation
target across
[Table 2](#S7.T2 "In 7.2 Benchmark Landscape Across Modalities ‣ 7 Evaluation and Applications ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory").
State tracking is increasingly considered in personalized, interactive,
and embodied settings. Conflict resolution and evidence insufficiency
remain sparsely evaluated, however, and memory-grounded action is
concentrated in GUI and embodied benchmarks. Consequently,
retrieval-centric applications are better represented in current
benchmarks than applications that require persistent state maintenance,
conflict handling, or memory-grounded action. Current evaluation
therefore establishes whether experience can be recovered more
consistently than whether it remains valid, sufficient, and actionable.

Modality-specific evaluation is strongest for structure native to each
input stream. Image benchmarks emphasize visual details, entities, and
state changes ([Jiang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib84); [Ren et al.,
2026](#bib.bib176)); video benchmarks emphasize temporal localization
and multi-event reasoning ([Yang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib263); [Liu et
al., 2026e](#bib.bib130)); audio and speech benchmarks examine long-form
retrieval, speaker- and acoustic-level retention, and stateful
interaction ([Someki et al., 2026](#bib.bib189); [Yao et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib267)). GUI and embodied benchmarks instead focus on
interface, spatial, object, and task states ([Yadav et al.,
2026](#bib.bib259); [Liu et al., 2026c](#bib.bib128)). Audio evaluation
nevertheless remains predominantly recall- or transcription-oriented,
with limited coverage of persistent correction, personalized response,
speaker conflict, abstention, and memory-grounded action.

Lifecycle coverage remains concentrated on persistence and retrieval in
T1 Static Memory; state-update and experience-reuse tasks probe T2
Dynamic Memory, but usually under stable policies. A Learn label
therefore does not establish T3 Self-Evolving Memory unless deployment
feedback produces persistent changes to a reusable memory-management
policy ([Zeng et al., 2026](#bib.bib278); [Liu et al.,
2026e](#bib.bib130)). Thus, although current benchmarks cover important
application-facing retrieval capabilities, their lifecycle coverage
remains incomplete. The main gaps lie in conflict and uncertainty
handling, source provenance, end-to-end memory attribution, policy
adaptation, and memory-grounded visual generation.

## 8 Challenges and Outlook

The preceding sections show that long-term multimodal agent memory
depends on three coupled concerns: what experience is retained and how
it is represented, how that memory is maintained as new evidence
arrives, and how its logical operations are realized under finite system
resources. Their interaction becomes more consequential over long
trajectories, changing environments, and shared deployments. We
therefore distinguish challenges in formation and representation,
challenges in memory management, and tensions between the two, followed
by deployment-oriented evaluation and open infrastructure problems. The
infrastructure discussion builds on
[Section 6](#S6 "6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
and focuses on how the assumptions and guarantees of the analyzed
mechanisms can be integrated under sustained deployment.

### 8.1 Multimodal Memory Formation and Representation

Memory formation determines not only what information is retained, but
also what can still be recovered after the original experience has been
transformed, what can later be located and changed inside the resulting
representation, and how far any of this has been worked out beyond the
modalities that dominate current practice. Current systems use a wide
range of source, explicit, latent, and parametric representations, yet
important questions remain about what each of them should preserve, what
structure each should expose, and whether the answers established for
visual experience carry over to other modalities.

#### 8.1.1 Recovering Supporting Evidence

Abstraction should move from lossy compression toward recoverable
representation. As previous sections show, modality-specific encodings,
textual, structured, latent, and parametric memories can all remove
information that remains available in source-level evidence.
Source-linked designs introduced in
[Section 3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Hybrid Representations ‣ 3 Axis I: Formation and Representation ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
partly address this problem by preserving links from derived memories
back to supporting observations. The remaining question is what
information should be preserved during formation so that this
recoverability is reliable.

Existing systems use different combinations of timestamps ([Wang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib226)), source identifiers ([Feng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib46)), entity links ([Long et al., 2026](#bib.bib143)),
spatial references ([Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib135)), and pointers to
supporting observations ([Lin et al., 2026d](#bib.bib124)). However, a
substantial portion of the analyzed architectures do not retain a usable
route back to the evidence from which their memories were formed. Among
those that do, the route is often simply that the source was never
abstracted away, rather than a link deliberately carried by a derived
memory, and where such links do exist they differ in what they record.
Provenance is therefore seldom a designed property of the
representation. A useful direction is to define a minimal provenance
bundle for formed memories, containing enough information to identify
where a memory came from, how it was produced, and what evidence
supports it. The required fields may differ across modalities and
representation types, but provenance should be treated as part of the
representation itself rather than as optional metadata.

Recoverable representation does not require every source observation to
be retained indefinitely. Instead, memory formation should make explicit
which information may be discarded and which supporting evidence must
remain reachable for later inspection or reinterpretation. This would
make abstraction more controlled without requiring all downstream
memories to preserve the full original experience. What remains open is
how to make this decision. Current systems use different rules ([Shen et
al., 2026](#bib.bib183); [Liu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib126)), but a better
criterion should balance retention cost against the need to verify or
correct information later.

#### 8.1.2 Finding and Updating Specific Memory

Formed memory should expose the units that memory management acts on.
While recoverability asks whether a memory can be traced back to its
supporting evidence, semantic addressability asks whether specific
content can be identified and changed within the representation itself.
Explicit textual and structured records provide such units by
construction, which is why they support revision and conflict resolution
most directly ([Bo et al., 2026](#bib.bib15)). Semantic addressability
remains rare outside these representations. The difficulty is sharpest
in latent and parametric memory, which is compact and integrates
directly with the model’s computation but does not expose content as
separately identifiable units by construction. An update to such memory
may therefore reach information it was not intended to change, and the
system may not be able to identify which part of memory is responsible
for a particular behaviour.

This limitation appears in the corpus as a pattern rather than only as
an argument.
[Section 5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 Corpus-Level Patterns Across the Two Axes ‣ 5 Cross-Axis Analysis ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
shows that every architecture evolving a memory-management policy at
deployment time maintains an explicit cross-represented component, and
that none whose memory is only latent or only parametric does so. The
absence is not a matter of these systems being static: most latent-only
architectures do update their memory state under a fixed policy. What
they lack is not dynamism, but clearly identifiable units over which
memory-management decisions can be attributed, inspected, and revised.
Source-preserving memory shows the same absence despite being
addressable in another sense, and the contrast is instructive: its units
can be identified perceptually, by time or position, yet still not at
the semantic level at which a write or retention decision is made. The
obstacle is therefore not distributed representation as such, but the
absence of units that correspond to what a policy decides about.

Parametric memory can already be divided into separable modules
associated with different experiences, modalities, or tasks, as in
adapter banks that hold per-task procedures ([Si et al.,
2026](#bib.bib188)), per-video parameters ([Suri et al.,
2026](#bib.bib200)), or modality-specific edits ([Seong et al.,
2025](#bib.bib180)). This makes parts of a distributed representation
easier to locate and manipulate, but it has not so far produced semantic
addressability: among the analyzed systems that organize memory this
way, the few that evolve a management policy during deployment do so
through an explicit cross-represented component rather than through the
parameter store itself. Structured latent memory that binds persistent
state to identifiable slots or entities ([Chung et al.,
2026](#bib.bib32)) would be a further step in the same direction. What a
fuller answer requires is nonetheless clear: a distributed memory is
addressable in the sense that management needs only when the same unit
can be identified, revised on its own, and afterwards verified to have
changed while the rest of memory did not. The open question is whether
that combination can be achieved without losing the compactness and
direct model integration that motivate latent and parametric memory in
the first place.

### 8.2 Multimodal Memory Management

[Section 4](#S4 "4 Axis II: Memory Management ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
describes how memory changes after formation, from fixed retrieval to
persistent maintenance and feedback-driven policy evolution. The
challenges collected here concern two questions that arise once memory
is allowed to change over time: how the system should keep its memory up
to date as new experience arrives, and how the policies that manage
memory can themselves improve from feedback.

#### 8.2.1 Maintaining Up-to-Date Memory

Memory maintenance should move from recording change toward keeping
track of which state is still valid. New observations can be appended,
existing memories can be revised, and repeated evidence can be merged,
but these operations do not by themselves tell the system whether an
older state still holds, has been replaced, or should be kept only as
history. This becomes especially important in multimodal settings, where
evidence about the same object, event, or user may arrive at different
times and through different modalities. The difficulty here concerns
observations of the same state that arrive separately, not disagreement
among the stored representations derived from them.

A timestamp records when an observation was made, not how long what it
asserts remains true. In multimodal settings the two can come apart in a
particular way. A visual observation may show where an object was seen,
while a later instruction may report that it has moved. A new image may
correct an earlier description, while the older observation remains
useful as historical evidence. Where staleness is handled at all, it is
often handled by removing or replacing the outdated record ([Yeo et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib269)), or by checking a cached state against a fresh
observation at the moment of use ([Liu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib140)),
rather than by representing how long a belief remains valid.

A promising direction is to explicitly model this status within the
memory management process. A memory may be marked as current,
historical, superseded, uncertain, or still valid alongside another
state. Such decisions may depend on the source and reliability of new
evidence rather than on recency alone. They may also need to distinguish
when an observation is received from when the event it describes
actually happened. What remains open is how an agent should decide when
new evidence replaces an older state, when both should coexist, and when
uncertainty should be preserved rather than resolved.

#### 8.2.2 Self-Improving Memory Management

Keeping memory up to date assumes that the rules for doing so are
already good enough. The next challenge is to improve those rules from
experience. As
[Section 4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 T3: Self-Evolving Memory ‣ 4 Axis II: Memory Management ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
describes, feedback-driven memory management changes how memories are
written, maintained, or retrieved during deployment. This is different
from optimizing a controller during training and then freezing it: once
deployment begins, a frozen controller continues to apply a stable
policy even as the memory contents change.

Current policy evolution is concentrated on retrieval, while changes to
write and maintenance policies remain much less common. One likely
reason is that retrieval receives relatively direct feedback: the system
can often observe whether retrieved memory helped the next answer or
action. The effect of an earlier write, merge, revision, or forgetting
decision may appear much later, and in a multimodal agent it may not
appear in the same modality at all. A memory written from a visual
observation may be revealed as wrong only by a later instruction, by an
observation in another modality, or by the failure of an action taken on
its basis. Credit therefore has to travel across both time and modality
before it can reach the decision that should change.

A useful direction is to connect later success and failure back to the
memory decision that most likely caused it. This would allow
feedback-driven improvement to extend beyond retrieval without treating
every downstream error as evidence that the entire memory policy should
change. What remains open is how to assign delayed and cross-modal
feedback to earlier memory decisions while separating their effects from
the many other operations that occur in between.

### 8.3 Representation–Management Tensions in Multimodal Memory

[Section 5](#S5 "5 Cross-Axis Analysis ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
shows that representation and memory management cannot be designed
independently. What a memory preserves limits what later operations can
inspect, change, verify, or remove. At the same time, the way memory is
managed determines which parts of a representation remain useful over
long interactions. The challenges here arise from this coupling. They
are not problems of representation or management alone, but cases in
which one limits what the other can do.

#### 8.3.1 Editable Representations without Loss of Detail

Multimodal memory should preserve perceptual detail without making later
correction difficult. Source observations and modality-specific
representations retain information that may disappear after an image,
video, trajectory, or other observation is converted into text or
structure. Yet the same abstraction that loses detail often makes memory
easier to revise. A textual fact or graph entry can be changed directly,
while correcting one semantic detail inside a long video, a distributed
latent state, or a parameter update is much less straightforward. What a
representation preserves therefore limits how precisely memory can later
be maintained, both in how narrowly an update can be scoped and in how
directly its result can be checked.

Hybrid and source-linked designs reduce this tension by keeping an
abstract memory together with a route back to supporting evidence ([Wang
et al., 2026e](#bib.bib218); [Fan et al., 2026a](#bib.bib42)). But
coexistence alone does not settle the problem. An abstract record can
become outdated while the source observation remains valid as historical
evidence. A new observation may also contradict the current abstraction
without making the older evidence useless. The system must then decide
which layer should guide current behavior and when the source should be
reopened rather than trusting the abstraction.

A useful direction is to combine editable memory state with recoverable
modality-specific evidence and an explicit rule for moving between them.
Routine updates can operate on compact textual or structured state,
while uncertain or high-impact changes can return to the supporting
image, video, audio segment, or trajectory for verification. What
remains open is how much source detail must stay reachable for later
correction without making long-term memory expensive to maintain.

#### 8.3.2 Selective Evidence Retention for Verifiable Memory

Verifiable memory should not require every past observation to remain
available forever. Retained source evidence, provenance, version
history, and checkpoints make memory changes easier to inspect and
reverse. In multimodal memory, however, the cost of keeping this support
depends strongly on what form the evidence takes. A short textual
record, selected image frames, a long video, an audio segment, a 3D
trajectory, and a latent or parametric checkpoint impose very different
storage and processing costs. The representation therefore limits how
much evidence a management system can realistically keep for later
verification.

Current systems usually make this choice implicitly through what their
memory architecture happens to retain, rather than through an explicit
policy for verification. Some retain source observations ([Wang et al.,
2026j](#bib.bib223)), some retain only derived records ([Gao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib48)), and others keep checkpoints or structured state ([Gu
et al., 2024](#bib.bib54)). What is often missing is a rule for which
evidence deserves long-term retention, which evidence can be compressed,
and which updates are important enough to justify preserving an earlier
version.

A useful direction is selective verification. Lightweight provenance can
remain available for most memories, while expensive source evidence or
checkpoints are kept only when later inspection is likely to matter.
High-impact revisions, uncertain memories, or information supported by
conflicting modalities may justify stronger evidence retention than
routine observations. The open problem is how to predict this need
before the future correction or dispute actually occurs. A system that
keeps too little loses the ability to verify its memory, while one that
keeps everything gives up much of the benefit of abstraction.

#### 8.3.3 Policy Adaptation with Preserved Evidence Grounding

Self-improving memory management should not silently change what
evidence the agent relies on. As
[Section 4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 T3: Self-Evolving Memory ‣ 4 Axis II: Memory Management ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
describes, a policy may evolve how memory is written, maintained, or
retrieved. In a multimodal system, such a change can also alter the path
through which information reaches the agent. A retrieval policy may
gradually favor textual summaries over visual evidence, a write policy
may compress one modality more aggressively, or a maintenance policy may
preserve some forms of memory while discarding others. Management
evolution can therefore change not only performance, but also which
representations continue to support that performance.

This creates a stability problem that task accuracy alone may not
reveal. A revised policy can maintain or even improve short-term answers
while relying less on the modality that originally grounded them. For
example, a system may answer correctly from a cached textual summary
while rarely reopening the visual evidence from which that summary was
formed. If the summary later becomes wrong, the loss of that evidence
path may only become visible much later. Current policy-evolution
methods rarely evaluate whether adaptation changes the balance of
evidence used across representations.

A useful direction is to evaluate policy changes together with the
evidence paths they alter. Before a new policy is accepted, the system
should check not only whether downstream performance improves, but also
whether access to supporting modalities and representations has been
weakened. This may require tracking which memory paths support important
decisions and comparing that use before and after adaptation. What
remains open is how much change in evidence use is healthy adaptation
and when it becomes a loss of grounding that should block or reverse the
policy update.

#### 8.3.4 Sustaining Memory without Losing the Ability to Forget

Long-term memory should remain bounded without losing control over what
can be removed. The difficulty depends on representation. Retained
images, videos, audio, and trajectories grow with experience; structured
memory grows with entities, events, and relations; a bank of adapters
can grow with tasks or episodes; and a fixed-size latent state faces a
different problem, because new information must compete with what is
already encoded. Representation therefore determines what grows, while
memory management determines how that growth can be contained.

Existing systems use operations such as consolidation ([Rasheed and
Kabtoul, 2026](#bib.bib173)), compression ([Li et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib104)), eviction ([Lin et al., 2026c](#bib.bib123)), decay
([Sun et al., 2026b](#bib.bib196)), and forgetting ([Liu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib133)), but sustained memory growth under a fixed budget
remains weakly addressed. A useful direction is representation-aware
budgeting. The system should not apply one retention rule to every
memory form. Source evidence may be sampled or compressed, structured
records may be merged, latent capacity may need to be reallocated, and
parametric modules may need consolidation or removal. The hard part is
deciding what can be reduced without destroying information whose value
will only become clear later.

Capacity is only one reason to remove memory. Some information may need
to disappear because it is outdated, corrected, or explicitly deleted.
In a multimodal system, that information may already have spread from a
source observation into a caption, embedding, graph node, summary,
latent state, or parameter update. Removing one copy therefore does not
establish that the information is gone. This also creates a direct
tension with
[Section 8.3.2](#S8.SS3.SSS2 "8.3.2 Selective Evidence Retention for Verifiable Memory ‣ 8.3 Representation–Management Tensions in Multimodal Memory ‣ 8 Challenges and Outlook ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory"):
verification benefits from retaining evidence and version history, while
deletion may require the same evidence and history to disappear.

A useful direction is to specify forgetting as a cross-representation
outcome rather than as the removal of a single record. Provenance and
derivation links can identify the captions, embeddings, structured
entries, summaries, or parameter modules that may carry the targeted
information, but locating a derivative does not guarantee that the
information can be selectively erased from it. The memory policy must
determine which information should become unavailable, which unrelated
knowledge should remain, and how the outcome can be verified. This also
makes the tension with reversibility explicit: retaining an earlier
version may support correction but conflict with a removal requirement.
The open representational problem is especially difficult for latent
states and shared parameters, where the targeted information is not
separately addressable.
[Section 6.6](#S6.SS6 "6.6 Consistency and Coordination ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
examines relevant coordination mechanisms, while
[Section 8.5](#S8.SS5 "8.5 Memory Infrastructure and Efficiency ‣ 8 Challenges and Outlook ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
addresses how a declared removal reaches replicas and active derivatives
and when that operation can be considered complete.

### 8.4 Deployment-Oriented Memory Evaluation

Evaluation determines which forms of progress become visible. Current
benchmarks establish increasingly broad coverage across modalities and
tasks, yet long-term memory is ultimately valuable as a process that
preserves, updates, accesses, and applies experience under continuing
interaction. Future evaluation should expose this process, stress it
over sustained horizons and bounded resources, and test it under the
operating conditions faced by deployed agents.

#### 8.4.1 Lifecycle-Aware Evaluation

Multimodal memory evaluation should move from outcome-level scoring
toward stage-resolved diagnosis. Many existing benchmarks summarize
performance with final answer accuracy or task success, including
long-video reasoning and interactive visual-recall settings ([Long et
al., 2026](#bib.bib143); [Tang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib203)). These
scores establish whether the complete system succeeded, while leaving
the origin of failure unresolved. Recent benchmarks demonstrate the
value of richer supervision through evidence annotations, update points,
retrieval judgments, feedback-reuse tests, and memory-specific execution
metrics ([Liu et al., 2026c](#bib.bib128); [Liu et al.,
2026e](#bib.bib130); [Chai et al., 2026](#bib.bib17); [Liu et al.,
2026d](#bib.bib129)). A lifecycle-aware protocol can organize such
signals around four observable stages.

##### Formation.

Evaluation should determine whether the agent identifies the parts of an
experience that will matter later and forms faithful memory from them.
Useful process metrics include coverage of gold memory points,
correctness and supportedness of written records, rates of hallucinated
or irrelevant entries, preservation of source links, and retention of
task-relevant visual, acoustic, spatial, and temporal detail. These
signals evaluate selective writing and representation quality before
later retrieval can conceal their failures.

##### Maintenance.

Evaluation should track whether persistent memory remains valid as new
evidence arrives. Intermediate metrics can measure successful
incorporation of current state, rejection or supersession of stale
records, conflict resolution, faithfulness of consolidation, and
consistency across source, textual, structured, latent, or parametric
representations. Versioned memory snapshots and annotated state
transitions can further reveal when an initially correct memory becomes
corrupted during update, compression, or reorganization.

##### Access.

Evaluation should assess whether the evidence required by the current
decision is recovered from the appropriate memory path. Evidence recall,
precision, ranking quality, temporal or spatial localization,
cross-modal coverage, and retrieval latency expose distinct access
failures. Comparing ordinary retrieval with oracle evidence also
separates limitations of memory access from those of the downstream
reasoner.

##### Utilization.

Evaluation should verify that accessed memory actually guides the
response, plan, or action. Evidence-conditioned correctness, source
attribution, adherence to the current state under conflict,
action–outcome consistency, and recovery after feedback provide
process-level measures of memory use. Counterfactual removal or
replacement of retrieved evidence can further test whether an apparently
correct output causally depends on memory. For generative agents,
utilization should additionally test whether retrieved constraints
preserve entity, style, temporal state, and world consistency, and
whether subsequent memory updates propagate coherently through later
revisions of the generated artifact.

Few benchmarks expose all four stages, and complete lifecycle
supervision is especially scarce for native multimodal evidence.
Establishing shared trajectory annotations and stage-level metrics would
make memory failures localizable, allow process rewards to target the
operation that failed, and support meaningful comparison among
architectures whose final accuracy may be similar for very different
reasons.

#### 8.4.2 Long-Horizon and Resource-Aware Evaluation

Long-horizon evaluation should measure sustained memory quality under
the resource pressure created by accumulating multimodal experience. The
field has begun to extend temporal scale: M3-Bench evaluates videos
averaging roughly half an hour ([Long et al., 2026](#bib.bib143)),
StreamArena reaches hour-scale causal streams ([Zhang et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib286)), EgoLife records a week of shared daily experience
([Yang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib263)), and EgoMonth spans 20–120 days of
egocentric observations ([Chen et al., 2026f](#bib.bib25)). This
progression brings evaluation closer to the timescale of persistent
assistants. Continuous deployment protocols with interleaved writing,
maintenance, querying, and feedback remain much less developed; even
long multi-session histories are often frozen and queried offline ([Ren
et al., 2026](#bib.bib176)).

##### Resource pressure.

As the observation stream grows, a memory system consumes persistent
storage, write-time computation, retrieval bandwidth, model context, and
response time. Evaluation should therefore impose explicit budgets and
report memory size and growth rate, ingestion throughput and lag,
retrieval latency, token or compute cost per unit of experience, and the
fraction of source evidence retained at each fidelity level. Early
studies already expose large differences in write–read latency and
execution cost across memory designs ([Liu et al., 2026c](#bib.bib128);
[Liu et al., 2026d](#bib.bib129)); standardized budgets would turn these
isolated measurements into comparable operating constraints. Systems
accounting should also distinguish the size of logical memory from the
total physical footprint of its replicas, indices, cached execution
states, and temporary buffers. In addition to end-to-end latency and
memory quality, experiments should report peak accelerator occupancy,
transferred bytes, and the costs of materialization, decompression, and
recomputation. Warm-cache and cold-cache conditions should be identified
separately, and construction or background write-back should not be
treated as free when their costs are shifted outside the query interval.
These measurements connect the quality–resource frontier to the
mechanisms in
[Section 6](#S6 "6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
without reducing memory quality to cache hit rate.

##### Longitudinal degradation.

A bounded memory must continually decide what to preserve, consolidate,
or forget. Its evaluation should trace accuracy, evidence recall, update
correctness, grounding, and action quality as a function of elapsed
time, accumulated experience, and available memory. Context-length
analyses and time-stratified forgetting curves provide useful starting
points ([Ren et al., 2026](#bib.bib176); [Shi et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib185)), while deployment-oriented protocols should also
reveal delayed corruption, retrieval slowdown, representation drift, and
the compounding effect of early writing errors on later decisions. The
central comparison is the quality–resource frontier: how reliably a
system preserves useful, verifiable memory as its operating horizon
grows under a fixed budget.

#### 8.4.3 Real-World Deployment

Deployment evaluation should reproduce the conditions under which
multimodal memory must operate continuously. Real environments combine
strict response deadlines, imperfect sensing, asynchronous feedback,
open-ended tasks, and changes in users and worlds. Benchmarks
increasingly incorporate real egocentric recordings, interactive
interfaces, and evolving state ([Yang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib263); [Chen
et al., 2026f](#bib.bib25); [Liu et al., 2026d](#bib.bib129); [Liu et
al., 2026c](#bib.bib128)), while most still isolate these factors within
curated data, controlled state transitions, or resettable environments.

##### Real-time operation.

An agent that recalls the correct evidence after the decision window has
passed cannot provide effective assistance. Evaluation should measure
end-to-end response latency, deadline-miss rate, proactive trigger
timing, and the delay between observation and query-visible memory
availability. RIVER couples memory accuracy with temporal distance and
response timing, while StreamArena measures query-to-answer latency
across routing, recall, external search, and inference ([Shi et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib185); [Zhang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib286)). Extending
these protocols to continuous memory writing and maintenance would
expose whether background processing can keep pace with the incoming
multimodal stream. For deployments requiring failure recovery, the time
to a recoverable commit and behavior after interrupted writes should be
measured separately under an explicit failure model; query visibility
alone does not establish durability.

##### Perceptual and environmental robustness.

Deployment streams contain motion blur, occlusion, poor lighting,
overlapping speech, sensor dropout, uncertain timestamps, and incomplete
or contradictory feedback. Systems also encounter devices, interfaces,
locations, speakers, and object appearances outside the distributions
represented in curated benchmarks. Evaluation should introduce
controlled corruptions alongside naturally noisy trajectories, vary
which modalities remain available, and test whether memory preserves
uncertainty, requests clarification, or abstains when the evidence is
insufficient. Robustness should be measured across both memory formation
and later reuse, since an unnoticed perceptual error can persist long
after the original observation has disappeared.

##### Continual user and world change.

Long-running agents must follow changing preferences, identities,
routines, goals, interface states, and physical environments. Evaluation
should present irregular state changes, delayed corrections, cross-modal
disagreement, and multiple users whose memories must remain separated.
The resulting metrics should capture adaptation delay, stale-memory use,
recovery after correction, cross-user contamination, and retention of
valid historical evidence. Such protocols would connect benchmark
success to the defining requirement of deployed memory: maintaining
reliable continuity while the world that memory describes continues to
change.

### 8.5 Memory Infrastructure and Efficiency

[Section 6](#S6 "6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
examines mechanisms for residency, restoration, reuse, materialization,
and coordination. The open systems problem is how their assumptions and
guarantees can compose over the lifetime of changing multimodal memory
under bounded resources. The directions below concern runtime decisions
and guarantees. They complement the representational and management
requirements in
[Section 8.3](#S8.SS3 "8.3 Representation–Management Tensions in Multimodal Memory ‣ 8 Challenges and Outlook ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
and the evaluation protocols in
[Section 8.4](#S8.SS4 "8.4 Deployment-Oriented Memory Evaluation ‣ 8 Challenges and Outlook ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory").

#### 8.5.1 Workflow-Responsive Residency and Data Movement

Program- and workflow-aware systems already exploit execution phase,
relative idleness, and anticipated reuse ([Kang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib92); [Xia et al., 2026b](#bib.bib248); [Pan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib165)). The next question is how placement and transfer
execution should respond when those signals change while data is in
flight. TokenCake, for example, already triggers an immediate upload
when a tool returns earlier than predicted ([Bian et al.,
2027](#bib.bib13)). A broader runtime contract should address branch
cancellation, overlapping readers, and reprioritization across storage
tiers: which transfers can be interrupted, which must drain, when
staging buffers can be reused, and whether completed chunks remain
useful. Research should connect transfer granularity and queue depth to
bounded wasted traffic and resumption delay, rather than treating
cancellation as an instantaneous reversal of offload.

Compression should also be optimized over repeated use rather than a
single transfer. Building on the transport and compute–load mechanisms
in
[Section 6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 Data Movement, Compression, and Reconstruction ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory"),
future designs should jointly account for encoding, decompression,
temporary storage, layout conversion, and the number of expected
restorations. Incremental restoration may reduce startup delay, but
finer transfer units add metadata and scheduling overhead. Quality
analysis should distinguish repeatedly decoding one unchanged compressed
artifact from repeatedly re-encoding or approximately reconstructing its
outputs; only the latter introduces an additional chain of potentially
accumulating approximation. The objective is a lifetime cost–quality
trade-off, not network-byte reduction alone.

#### 8.5.2 Dependency-Aware Reuse and Scheduling

The dependency assumptions of prefix caching and selective recomputation
in
[Section 6.4](#S6.SS4 "6.4 Indexing, Reuse, and Scheduling ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
become harder to track when memory is revised, reordered, cropped, or
materialized through a different model interface. Future work should
investigate compact dependency descriptions that connect execution
artifacts to their source versions and relevant transformations, such as
preprocessing, encoder or adapter versions, prompt composition,
positions, and attention configuration. These descriptions should
distinguish exact reuse from empirically validated approximation and
permit selective invalidation or reconstruction. An unresolved trade-off
is granularity: coarse dependencies cause unnecessary recomputation,
while fine-grained tracking can cost more than the computation it saves.

Scheduling should use this information without collapsing relevance into
cache locality. Preble establishes the value of balancing prefix reuse
with worker load ([Srivatsa et al., 2025](#bib.bib193)); multimodal
memory introduces additional choices among available evidence
representations and materialization paths. Research should optimize
worker selection, cache admission, prefetching, and reconstruction
jointly, subject to the evidence, freshness, and quality requirements of
the task. Reuse value must include validation overhead, expected
remaining uses before invalidation, and interference with other
programs. A high hit rate is not a sufficient objective when the hits
are expensive to restore, likely to be invalidated before further use,
or available only for evidence that is less appropriate to the current
decision.

#### 8.5.3 Coordinating Materialization and Write-back

Read-side acceleration can shift cost into memory construction rather
than eliminate it. Existing workload characterization separates
construction, retrieval, and generation costs, while FOLIO illustrates
asynchronous construction with a recent-evidence path ([Omri et al.,
2026](#bib.bib162); [Fan et al., 2026a](#bib.bib42)). Future systems
should jointly schedule foreground inference and background encoding,
summarization, indexing, or adapter production. The key decisions are
when to materialize expensive artifacts, when to defer work until demand
is known, and how to prevent persistent write backlogs from making new
experience unavailable. These decisions should consider expected reuse
and invalidation, not just instantaneous GPU utilization.

Such orchestration also needs representation-specific fallbacks. When a
compact record is not ready, a runtime may expose retained source
evidence; when a model-specific artifact is incompatible, it may
reconstruct a compatible form from an authorized source. These
alternatives are not semantically interchangeable and should operate
within the memory policy’s requirements, rather than silently replacing
evidence to meet a latency target. Research should determine when eager
materialization, lazy reconstruction, or incremental publication
provides the best balance of responsiveness, groundedness, and
recoverability. Systems evaluation in
[Section 8.4](#S8.SS4 "8.4 Deployment-Oriented Memory Evaluation ‣ 8 Challenges and Outlook ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
should account for the costs incurred on both sides of this read–write
boundary.

#### 8.5.4 Cross-Layer Consistency, Recovery, and Revocation

The scoped guarantees in
[Section 6.6](#S6.SS6 "6.6 Consistency and Coordination ‣ 6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
motivate explicit publication and recovery contracts across artifacts.
Future work should specify whether a read requires a consistent
snapshot, read-your-writes visibility, or bounded staleness, and how
these requirements span source media, semantic records, retrieval
indices, and derived execution state. The coordination granularity need
not be the entire memory bank; a versioned set of dependent artifacts
may be sufficient. The challenge is to expose a coherent read path while
expensive derivatives are being rebuilt, without globally blocking
unrelated requests.

Durability should be specified separately from logical retention and
query visibility. For deployments that require recovery from failures,
research should identify which source records, versions, and
transformation results must be committed, which caches can be
reconstructed, and how interrupted write-back can resume without
duplicating or exposing incomplete records. Preserving source media
alone may not reproduce a prior stochastic summary or parameter update.
The required guarantee must therefore distinguish recovery of the exact
previous artifact from reconstruction of a newly generated alternative.

Deletion and permission changes extend coordination to already
materialized state. Whereas
[Section 8.3.4](#S8.SS3.SSS4 "8.3.4 Sustaining Memory without Losing the Ability to Forget ‣ 8.3 Representation–Management Tensions in Multimodal Memory ‣ 8 Challenges and Outlook ‣ Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory")
asks what must be forgotten and how to verify that outcome, the
infrastructure question is how a declared removal propagates through
replicas, indices, summaries, contexts, caches, and retained versions.
Future work should define a completion boundary and distinguish
preventing new retrieval from retiring active derivatives and reclaiming
storage. Collaborative Memory’s retrieval-time access control provides
one boundary, not a demonstrated solution for all downstream artifacts
([Rezazadeh et al., 2025](#bib.bib177)). Dependency metadata can
identify retirement targets, but cannot by itself establish semantic
erasure from a distributed latent state or shared model parameters.

MemOS proposes common abstractions for heterogeneous memory resources,
while MemoryOS organizes hierarchical memory for agent interaction ([Li
et al., 2025b](#bib.bib117); [Kang et al., 2025](#bib.bib93)). Building
on such efforts, the objective should be interoperable contracts for
identity, version, provenance, compatibility, and lifetime—not a
universal representation that erases modality-specific semantics. The
central open problem is to make their guarantees compose under finite
resources and partial failure while preserving the evidence needed for
future reasoning and correction.

## 9 Conclusion

The central question of multimodal agent memory is what evidence to
retain from heterogeneous multimodal experience, how to represent it for
subsequent reasoning and action, and how to keep it valid over time. Our
framework characterizes multimodal agent memory along two axes:
Formation and Representation, and Memory Management. Axis I classifies
the operative representation through which retained experience becomes
available to downstream computation; Axis II distinguishes T1 Static
Memory, T2 Dynamic Memory and T3 Self-Evolving Memory. Joint analysis of
the two axes shows that representation constrains the accessibility,
revisability, verifiability, and recoverability of memory. The
coexistence of multiple representations further requires maintaining
provenance links, temporal validity, and cross-representation
consistency, and updating memory state is not equivalent to evolving the
management policy. Current systems remain dominated by fixed memory and
memory updating through stable policies. Online policy evolution,
bounded lifelong memory, governed forgetting, and lifecycle-aware
evaluation remain underdeveloped. At the systems level, current
infrastructure lacks unified mechanisms for efficiently and consistently
storing, restoring, and reusing memory under finite resource
constraints; while existing benchmarks remain insufficient to establish
whether memories remain valid, sufficient, and actionable throughout the
full memory lifecycle. Together, these challenges point toward a
multimodal memory system for long-term operation that preserves
verifiable and recoverable multimodal evidence under bounded resources,
maintains temporally evolving and cross-representation-consistent memory
states, and uses continual feedback to improve its memory-management
policies.
